utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. First of all, I have to say that we're sitting under the provisions of Rule 15 bis this morning, in the absence of Judge Kwon, who is unavoidably detained. But before we start with the testimony of Radomir Kezunovic, there are four procedural matters that I would like to deal with. The first is an oral decision on the admission of documents bearing 65 ter 11701. The first, it's an oral decision. On the 1st of November, 2010, the accused used page 86 of the Prosecution document with Rule 65 ter 11701 during his cross-examination of Prosecution Witness Anton Brennskag. This page, which is at transcript 8770, line 3, forms part of the report prepared by Prosecution Witness Robert Donia, was admitted into evidence by the Chamber, and should have been assigned an Exhibit number, D855 at the time (transcript page 8771, line 8). However, due to an oversight, it was never assigned an exhibit number and consequently does not appear as admitted in e-court. Given that the Exhibit D855 has been assigned to a different document, the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to assign the next available defence exhibit number to page 86 of the document with Rule 65 ter 11701, and to record that it is admitted into evidence. There is also an addendum to the decision of the accused, 9th of March, 2011 motion to make oral arguments made available to the public. On the 4th of May, 2011, the Chamber issued a decision on the accused's 9th March 2011 motion to make oral arguments available to the public, in which it ordered the Registry to lift the confidentiality of the portions of the transcript in which a Rule 70 condition had been placed on part of Rupert Smith's testimony. In order to be comprehensive, the Chamber wishes to clarify that the instruction to lift the confidentiality of the said portion of Rupert Smith's testimony applies to both the written transcript and to the audio-visual record. There is also a motion to subpoena for interview General Delic and Brigadier Brdjanovic. In relation to the motion to subpoena those individuals, the Criminal Defence Section of Bosnia-Herzegovina has tried to contact both Mr. Delic and Mr. Brdjanovic to communicate the accused's request for an interview. General Delic was contacted. However, he refused to be interviewed by the accused or by his legal adviser. Efforts to contact Brigadier Brdjanovic were unsuccessful. In a supplemental submission filed on the 11th of April, 2011, the accused stated that he will seek a subpoena for General Delic, but he would file additional information if and when Brigadier Brdjanovic was contacted. Mr. Robinson, is there any update as to that last matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we've had no more contact from the office -- the Defence office in Bosnia, and we would ask that the Chamber issue an order or request to the Government of Bosnia to summon those individuals. I believe they'd indicated their capable of receiving a summons and can arrange contact with them in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Well, the Chamber will discuss that matter. The last matter I want to deal with is a motion for subpoena for interview of Christoph von Bezold. In the latest confidential correspondence from Germany regarding this motion, Germany stated that the German national law does not envisage a court ordering subpoena of a person for an informal interview realised by the legal adviser of the accused. Germany also states that it is prompted to inform Mr. von Bezold in writing of the accused's request. Now, those are matters which, although they are not in themselves confidential, again, Mr. Robinson, it would be useful for the Chamber to be informed of any further action you may be taking in light of that response from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We haven't heard anything from Mr. von Bezold, and we would like to be in contact with him directly. And so if we don't hear anything within the next few days, we planned on asking the German government to give us his contact details so we can determine whether he's willing to be interviewed. And we can get back to the Chamber on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: While you're on your feet, Mr. Robinson, is there anything further you wish to deal with or mention before we proceed to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton, is this your witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Any other matters that the OTP wishes to raise before we proceed to testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No. Then let the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours -- with your leave, Your Honours, I would like to express my greatest gratitude to the Trial Chamber and to the Office of the Prosecutor for their efforts invested in visiting Sarajevo and gaining an insight into our geography and the scene where all the developments took place. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, your acknowledgment to that is appreciated, Dr. Karadzic. It was a substantial visit, and I think it was appreciated by everyone who took part in it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the record, 65 ter 11701, which was just admitted by the Trial Chamber, will be assigned Exhibit D1250.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Let the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Can you give the Court your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radomir Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, if you would like to sit and make yourself comfortable. Then you'll be asked questions first by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kezunovic. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I do hear you, and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kezunovic, do you recall, in March 2004 and January 2008, giving statements to the Office of the Prosecutor on your observations and experiences during the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is it correct that you gave evidence last year, in July 2010, in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case here before this Tribunal, on those same observations and experiences?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that on 21 May of this year, 2011, you met with me and another member of the Office of the Prosecutor, during which time we discussed and finalised a statement amalgamating all that previously-recorded evidence, together with some additions and clarifications that you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. So I have that amalgamated statement in front of me, and I thank you for the opportunity you gave me to review my previous testimony and to bring some precision into some of the things that I previously stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, apart from some clarifications -- some further clarifications I think we're going to make here today, if I was to ask you the same questions which gave rise to the information contained in that amalgamated statement of 21 May, would your answers also be the same?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my answers would be absolutely identical as you can see them in the amalgamated statement dated 21st May this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, then could I ask that that statement, which is 65 ter 90242, be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2526, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a summary of that written evidence. Following the multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, this witness served as president of the Executive Board of Ilidza Municipality, and from January 1992 until late March or early April of that year, held the title of president of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza. In this capacity, he also held the post of president of two successive crisis staffs until he resigned all his official functions in April or May of 1992, turning his duties and responsibilities over to Mr. Nedjeljko Prstojevic. According to the witness, Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik were the first two men in the SDS and in the Republika Srpska, and kept this position until the end of the war. The witness describes the organisational structure of the SDS party, with specific reference to Ilidza and the administration for the city of Sarajevo. He gives evidence as to the methods of communication within and between the different levels of the SDS party, again particularly with respect to Ilidza. Information and instructions were mostly orally transmitted from the top down, either through Mr. Prstojevic, Mr. Velibor Ostojic, or other high-level officials who lived in the area of Ilidza. The witness confirms the proclamation of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza in January 1992. He describes the growing tension in the area and the constitution of the two crisis staffs -- two successive crisis staffs I've referred to in and for the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza. The witness describes Ilidza as the last municipality in Sarajevo where hostilities started. He talks about unrest and tensions in the area from as early as May 1991, and his efforts to avoid conflict by, among other things, encouraging dialogue between the national parties. He discusses his efforts to develop a proposal for the territorial reorganisation of Ilidza Municipality, taking into account not only the area's ethnic structure, but also its economy and infrastructure. Prior to the outbreak of conflict, he talks about arming in the area. The witness also speaks to the presence of paramilitary forces in Serbian Ilidza, as well as the situation for civilians in that municipality during the conflict. That's the summary of the written evidence, Your Honours. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that statement, Mr. Kezunovic, I'd like to ask you some questions by way of further clarifications. And if I'm not mistaken, is that a copy of that amalgamated statement that you have in front of you today?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, then. Perhaps I could do this by way of references to particular paragraphs. At paragraph 16 in that document, there is an incomplete sentence. Regarding Mr. Prstojevic, who you referred to earlier in the statement, you noted he was in a position to transfer information and organise activities about the SDS party activities at the top level. And the next sentence, which is the incomplete one, reads: "Sometimes it was Karadzic or Krajisnik's, sometimes Koljevic or Plavsic." Now, I wonder if you're able to complete the thought or to finish that sentence for us.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When my words were transcribed with regard to the functioning of the party in Ilidza municipality, and the activities of the party leadership, I mentioned, as one of the possibilities, that the political information were transferred by Mr. Prstojevic, amongst others, and he was the one who attended the meetings where all the other persons that you mentioned in that sentence were present. And then he would come to Ilidza and he would inform us what was said, what suggestions were made, and what the activities of the party had been, and so on and so forth. So that was one of the ways we, in Ilidza, were informed about the activities by the top leaders of the party, and I'm talking about the year 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to go further: In paragraph 18, we see reference for the first time to the name Jovo Jovanovic from Vogosca, and you referred to him at several times -- several points in your statement. And I'd just like to ask you about this man, if you know whether he was a member of the SDS Main Board as well as the SDS Town Board.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The late Mr. Jovo Jovanovic, as far as I can remember, I'm sure that he was the president of the City Board of the SDS of the city of Sarajevo. And as far as I can remember, he was also a member of the Main Board of the SDS at the time. When I say "at the time," I mean 1990, 1991, up to the months of April or May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to go on to paragraph 20 of your statement, there you refer, actually, to a media report on a gathering on 6 May 1991, on Novakova Pecina, on Romanija Mountain, that Seselj's men were supposed to have attended. And I'd like to know: At that time, did you actually have a chance to see that media report?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about an event which happened on the 6th of May or the Day of St. George in 1991. And you say that these were media reports, but they were not. At the time, all the media in Sarajevo on that day, on the 6th of May, and I mean the radio and newspapers, they reported on a gathering that had taken place on Mount Romanija, in one part of Mount Romanija, the so-called Novakova Cave. That was a gathering, but not of Seselj's men. That was a gathering connected with St. George's Day. It is a traditional gathering of the population of the Romanija region around Novakova Cave, and that year the gathering was somewhat more extensive so that Vojislav Seselj and many other people who were politically engaged attended. I learned about the gathering from the Sarajevo media, but why I mentioned the whole thing was the reaction to the gathering which took place in the city of Sarajevo, and I described that reaction that was the harbinger of future concern and fears in Sarajevo, and especially in Ilidza, because that was the initial demonstration and show of weapons in response to that gathering that had taken place on Mount Romanija. So this is what I described under bullet point 20 of this amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just said that you didn't actually see a media report, but you knew, as I see from your answer, that Seselj -- Vojislav Seselj, among other people, attended that gathering. How do you know that he attended?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already told you, that was the main news on the radio and in newspapers that morning. The media reported about Mr. Seselj having attended the gathering around Novakova Cave. That was the top news for all those who were in a position to listen to radio reports or read newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you seen any video reports of that gathering?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a video footage on YouTube over the past five, six, or seven years. I subsequently saw a video footage depicting the event that took place on the 6th of May, 1991, at Novakova Cave. What I'm saying is that I saw all those subsequently. I didn't see any of those on the very 6th of May. That video footage appeared some five or six years after the event - in any case, after the war - and that is how I was able to complement my whole knowledge, or, rather, I was reminded of the event, which was the St. George's Day gathering on the 6th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dr. Karadzic attended that gathering?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Owing to that video footage, I noticed that Dr. Radovan Karadzic also attended that meeting. I didn't know it in 1991. However, when I saw the footage, I realised that Dr. Karadzic was also there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honours, with your leave and Dr. Karadzic's agreement, I'd like to play 65 ter 45100. That was a late-notified exhibit from yesterday afternoon that was discussed with the witness during the proofing on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I noticed that Dr. Karadzic has no objection, so that can be played.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, we're playing time code 9:21 to 13:36 from 65 ter 45100. It's been synchronised in Sanction, so I would ask my friends in the booth if they would be able to read from that transcript for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "My brothers and sisters, after half a century of Communist dictatorship, we have lived to see the day ... the Serbian national awareness, our pride and dignity, when we have rebuilt the Serbian accord and unity. And never again, my brothers and sisters, shall we allow someone to divide us and rip us apart and to make us confront each other ... " ... Of the world and our traditional enemies have joined forces against the Serbian people. They are attacking our women, our children, our elders who are helpless and unarmed. Our enemies from the West are trying to carry out a new genocide against the Serbian people. My Serbian brothers and sisters, it is up to us to put an end to this, and our enemies should know that not only shall the current victims be avenged, but we shall make them pay for all the previous ones as well, for they have dared once again to put the Ustasha knife against the Serbian throat. "That's right. "Especially you from the Serbian part of Bosnia, from the heroic Serbian Herzegovina, do not allow no one to separate and divide you. You have but one political party, the Serbian Democratic Party. You have your leadership, which was the first to prove itself in action, and which has saved the dignity of the all-Serbian brotherhood ... " ... The superior Ustasha forces that had them outnumbered, they showed them that the Serbian heroism has not died yet. The Serbian Chetnik detachments shall be active in all other regions of Western Serbia as well as in Serbia Krajina, Serbian Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem. We shall not give an inch of the Serbian land. The Slovenians can leave Yugoslavia. "That's right. "They were never neither our brothers or our friends. The Croats can leave too. They can separate Croatia, but we shall not give them an inch of the territory east of the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. "That's right. " ... glad to celebrate the St. George's Feast and brigand's early-morning gathering. This year, after only one year, we have changed the ... of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is you who have changed it without harming anyone. It was possible for the Serbs to get to their senses and become Serbs without getting anyone harm ... " ... in the past period, he had to hide his being he had to go to a place where ... This morning, when ... over our celebration cake, it seemed as if he caught old Slavs and gathered them in the woods to introduce them to Christianity again. "I'm not saying that things are great in Serbia. They should fight to diminish the power of the Socialist Party, but they should fight, as Mr. Seselj said, in a democratic manner, without damaging any of the Serbian interests, basic interests. Croatia has been militarised, gentlemen. If any other independent country armed itself to such an extent, by doubling or even quadrupling its armed forces, the United Nations would be in session day and night to find out why that is so. But they are surprised at us ... "... requests from the Bosnian Krajina for 30 years. Then we thought about it for a long time and gave our political consent for this regionalisation, the goal of which is to economically strengthen all the Serbian regions and Serbian areas that were neglected and underprivileged. Then our partners pointed out one thing to us, that it also has a great political significance. Well, fine, if it has a political significance, we will accept the political significance as well."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, is that the YouTube video that you saw?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the video that I had occasion to see on YouTube. I don't remember when it was that I saw it the first time, but, in any case, it was after 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2527, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also in this same paragraph, you refer to a document dated 23 July 1991, which is marked as Defence Exhibit D1178, minutes of an inter-party meeting between the national parties in Ilidza. Now, this document refers to your appeal to the population in Ilidza to preserve the common life there, and I wonder if that appeal has any relation to the unrest you've referred to otherwise in paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I've also -- I've already mentioned it. It was a reaction to the news that this St. George's Feast Day had been held. All the inhabitants of Ilidza, including me, were witnesses to an event that scared us all; namely, that a motorcade had been formed of about 15 or more vehicles. Most of them were taxis, and coming from Sarajevo, they passed through Ilidza, across the Ilidza Bridge, and by the municipality building there was shooting from the windows, volleys of gun-fire, and that was the first shooting in Ilidza. Since I was president of the Executive Council of Ilidza at the time, I felt it was my duty to react to something like that, this public show of weapons, and I convened the Executive Board, which is the local government of Ilidza, and we made a public statement condemning that and similar attempts to disturb law and order and cause unrest among the population. That was my first statement of that kind, but not the last. I used every opportunity I had from that time on, including this one you're asking about, 23rd July, at a meeting that included all the parties in power in Ilidza at the time, and I used this opportunity because it was an important meeting of prominent people in Ilidza, and I proposed to make a joint appeal to use the influence of political parties to get things under control again so that the events of 6th May never repeat themselves. That proposal was unanimously accepted, and it was one of my efforts, one of my attempts, something that I considered my duty to do, to act politically to try to prevent things from taking the wrong course, which eventually they did, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll move on to paragraphs 29 to 31, where you talk about the ethnic structure in Ilidza municipality. Now, first, in paragraph 29, you refer to people from Sandzak who were brought by buses to take part in the census, especially in Sokolovic Kolonija, and say that as a result you had an abnormal change in the ethnic structure as compared with 1991. You said in that paragraph that percentages of the Muslim population were being mechanically changed, and then you said -- then you say you had at that time 40.000 illegal structures in the area, built without housing permits. So I want to ask you a few clarifying questions about that paragraph. First of all, could you clarify, were these 40.000 structures you refer to built in the immediate area of Ilidza municipality or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, if you allow me one observation. It was a very broad question, from the census of Sokolovic Kolonija to the number of illegal structures. I'll try to answer in sequence. At that time, that is, up to 1992, and for 20 years before, from the 1970s to the 1990s, the city of Sarajevo always had this major problem of illegal building, building of structures without building permits issued by the city or the municipality. The incidence of that in Sarajevo was very high, and in all 10 city municipalities that number reached 40.000 houses that were built without any design documentation, without any building permits, and they were occupied by people who tried everything to legalise them. One of the possible ways to legalise such illegal structures was to take the opportunity of a census, such as the one in April 1992 [as interpreted]. That was the last census in Bosnia-Herzegovina, by the way. And during the census, the people would bring their families from their native places to be registered in places where they had built those illegal structures. The most numerous population of these newcomers was from Serbia, from the Sandzak area, and over those 20 years they had built these illegal houses, and they tried to register themselves in that place of residence in 1991 to meet one of the conditions to legalise their buildings. That's how this settlement in Ilidza came to be, like Sokoljevo in Novi Grad, like Sanac in Novo Sarajevo, like Buljak [phoen]. But to come back to Ilidza, such an illegal settlement was Sokolovic Kolonija, and comparing the 1991 census with the 1981 census, we noticed an anomaly in the results, in terms of the ethnic structure of the population. At that time, we called it a mechanical inflow of population rather than the normal demographic development, so that Ilidza municipality experienced this completely abnormal change in the ethnic structure over those 10 years, which we clearly saw by comparing the 1991 census with the 1981 census. How do I know this? I know this because at the time I was president of the Executive Board of the Ilidza Municipality and, ex officio, I was chairman of that commission in Ilidza whose legal duty it was to carry out the census. I'm sorry if I speak too fast. So it was my formal obligation in my position then to carry out the census. And during the census, it was noticed and it was common knowledge that people from Sokolovic Kolonija brought their families from Sandzak to participate in the census and be registered, and that resulted in a drastic and unnatural change in the ethnic structure of Ilidza, which eventually resulted in all the other consequences that were negative. That's a very long answer, but it's also the briefest way I can describe this situation in the territory of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a very long answer to not only the question I asked, but many that I didn't pose. Before I go on with a further question, I just want to note at page 16, line 18, you refer to the census as being in April 1992. In fact, that's not correct, is it? The census was in April 1991. And, I'm sorry, page 16 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: 1991, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd really like to encourage you, and we've spoken about this before, to try to speak not quite so quickly, Mr. Kezunovic, because sometimes speed of speech is how these misunderstandings occur. In relation to what you've just said, I have a -- as a result of the answer you've just given, I have a question I'd like to ask you, actually. I'm wondering, why would resettlement for economic or any other reason, regardless of whether the houses one settles in were built without building permits, why would resettlement be considered an anomalous, unnatural development, in terms of the ethnic structure of an area?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: You're right. If we talk about the normal development of population in any region, including Sarajevo, there's nothing controversial about that. But if, over a very short period of time, there is pronounced resettlement by any ethnic group, single ethnic group, like it happened in Ilidza, it raised indirect issues. And in Ilidza, for local administrations, it caused a whole new set of problems. I will try to explain why it's unnatural. Of course, if people of one ethnic group move in, they bring with them their cultural needs, their customs. And these newcomers, in their new environment, like in Ilidza, tried to practice their own way of life and their customs and traditions, and that raises issues with the traditional original environment. And we, in Ilidza, with this new changed ethnic structure, faced demands for the building of new places of worship. And I, as president of the municipal government, was faced with a request for building five or six new places of worship, including mosques. That's how this changed ethnic structure in Ilidza required to continue their traditions and their way of life, including the building of places of worship which had not been there in Ilidza before, and that was a legal issue that we, as the administration, had to deal with. And I must say that we did deal with those problems, and in most cases we managed to accommodate the newcomers, including their cultural and religious needs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a brief intervention in the transcripts. It's not "including mosques" in that line, but most of the places of worship that were required to be built were mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 40 of your statement and a very simple question. You talk about a meeting at the Holiday Inn which you attended, saying Prstojevic was there, Markovic was there, and Bosiljcic was there. My question is: Does that refer to -- does that name, Markovic, refer to Dragan Markovic, who's mentioned in paragraph 46 and further in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the late Dragan Markovic, commander of the Staff of the Territorial Defence of Ilidza Municipality. And the question is ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've answered [sic] the question, thank you, and you've given me the answer. Or I've asked you the question, you've provided the answer. And the man you refer to as Bosiljcic, is that the Ljubo Bosiljcic you refer to in paragraph 56?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's Mr. Ljubo Bosiljcic, deputy to the National Assembly, which is the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who became or was elected MP at the first multi-party elections held in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 24th November 1990. So he was an MP from Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you know whether he was also a member of the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move on a little bit to paragraph 46 and following, where there's a discussion about the crisis staffs in Ilidza. And it's going to take a while, but I think we'll get to some clarification in some dates through this. In paragraph 46, you talk about the formation of a crisis staff for Ilidza municipality in January 1992, saying that, formally speaking, you were the head. And then in paragraph 54, you said that, in fact, there were two crisis staffs: One constituted in January 1992 as a political organ of the SDS in Ilidza, succeeded in April 1992 by the Crisis Staff for the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza. You also said in paragraph 54 that at the very beginning, you were the head of the Crisis Staff for 15 to 20 days, and as a result of your position as the head of the Serbian -- and that was as a result of your position as head of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza. You said that after no more than 15 days, you sat with Mr. Prstojevic and told him that the job was his, and then at the end of April or the beginning of May 1992, you formally resigned all your functions. Can you follow all this -- the chain of the discussion so far?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But if you allow me, I would like to put it in the right chronology. The beginning was --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me, actually, maybe I can help you along the way with reference to a couple of documents. Then we can see if we can get the chronology in place. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we have a look --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the 3rd of January is the first event.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a look, please, at P2410, an order on the implementation of general mobilisation, signed on 6 April 1992 by Mr. Prstojevic, as president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see this document, on the left of the screen in front of you, in your own language?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please, can we go to the first page - thank you - in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've looked at this document in preparation for your testimony here today, have you not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Of course, that was the first time I saw these documents, during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could just move on to a further document now, D1193. It's assigned by Mr. Prstojevic on 10 April 1992, setting out the members of the Crisis Staff for the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see those documents in Serbian and in English on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document of 10 April 1992 sets out the members for the Crisis Staff for the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza, and I note, actually, your name doesn't appear on it. So now, looking at these documents, I wonder if they help you place in time when you might have had the conversation with Mr. Prstojevic handing over your functions.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the 3rd of January, when that Serbian Municipality of Ilidza was established as a preventive political act, and when I was elected as the president for that Serbian Ilidza Municipality, on the 3rd of January also a political crisis staff was also formed, and its task was to monitor security-related events, and otherwise they did not operate at all until the beginning of April 1992. With the formal establishment of the Crisis Staff, including the members on this list - I believe it was at an Assembly of the 4th or 5th of April - that Crisis Staff was formalised and it had an official role. It was established as a part of the official Ilidza Administration. And this conversation between me and Nedjeljko Prstojevic, when I asked him to allow me to hand over my duties, it was a private conversation between me and him, without any formalities, without any written documents. He accepted that I would continue to work in my own profession, which is engineering, and he would take over from me the other duties, including the role of the president of the Crisis Staff and my role in the municipality, and he did that. And these documents before us reflect this first period and the formal establishment of the Crisis Staff which would operate from April onwards and would later take specific decisions and specific actions on the ground. That's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can go back to the question I asked you. The question I asked you was, and I'll ask it a slightly different way --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did those documents, dated 6 and 10 April 1992, both signed by Mr. Prstojevic, as head of the Crisis Staff, help you in remembering or dating when you might have handed over your functions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly before this date, it's clear from this signature that this document from the Crisis Staff goes out under the name of Mr. Prstojevic. I cannot remember the exact date, but it was certainly sometime in mid-March, before these events, and that is why I am not listed here either as a nominee or a member of that Crisis Staff which operated without me as of mid-March.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just said that you -- that the Crisis Staff operated without you as of mid-March. But in light of that, I'd like to go back to a document you referred to in your written evidence. It's D1199, dated 21 April 1992, and it's a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza -- pardon me, it's dated 19 April 1992 -- in light of the imminent threat of war, and it's signed by Mr. Prstojevic. Now, if I could direct you to the top right-hand corner of this document, there's a notation there that says that the decision was re-examined on 21 April 1992, there was a vote on it, and of those present, 10-9 were in favour and there was one abstention, Kezunovic. So I wondering how this document and that notation fits in with what you've just said about how the Crisis Staff operated without you as of mid-March.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, look, I was still in Ilidza. The role of the president of the Crisis Staff was taken over by Mr. Prstojevic. He was leading that institution, and at that time I was still in Ilidza. The Executive Board still worked. I still participated in it, attended all its meetings, but not as the chairman of the Crisis Staff but a person who was part of that local government. And I attended this meeting, too, although I had not seen this document before, but I can confirm this. And even at meetings that I attended informally, not as a member of the Crisis Staff, I attended as president of the Executive Board. And I needed sometimes to get instructions, what to do and how, and at this meeting I was trying to influence the decisions taken by the Crisis Staff by opposing, even, some decisions and proposals that did not sound reasonable to me. And you have to bear in mind the context of the events that were going on in April 1992. It was my opinion that we should continue in our attempts, I mean the attempts of the whole government of Ilidza, to prevent misunderstandings or the beginning of hostilities, and we still expected that an understanding would be reached, in general terms, and we had great hopes in the Cutileiro-Carrington Agreements from Lisbon. We all expected that this agreement would be implemented and that an end would be put to all the disagreements in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And we all played our roles, including me. We opposed all the decisions that could have complicated the situation in Ilidza, and this decision of the Crisis Staff was one of those that I believed to be unreasonable.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to try and remind you, Mr. Kezunovic, to stay focused on my questions, because we are under some time constraints. I'd like to go now to paragraph 69 of your statement. There, you referred to a meeting in Ilidza held somewhere around the middle of April 1992, where the discussion was -- the discussion centred on where to establish the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, in that regard, I'd like to refer to a transcript of an intercepted conversation you reviewed in preparation for your testimony here today, and that's 65 ter 30682, an intercepted conversation between Jovo Jovanovic and Maksim Stanisic, both of whom have been referred to in your statement.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Mr. Jovanovic you've spoken about in your evidence today. Now, could we have 65 ter 30682, please. And while we're waiting for that, perhaps I could ask you: Did you listen to an audio recording of that conversation in preparation for testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I listened to that audio recording yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you recognise the voices of the speakers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised the voices of Mr. Jovo Jovanovic and Maksim Stanisic. They were the interlocutors in that intercepted conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Unless mistaken, the booth have not received this transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's not the conversation. I'd like 65 ter 30682, and you've got 30862 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for my friends in the booth, we won't be playing this intercept, we'll just be referring to the document. So no need for separate distribution of the transcripts, but thank you for alerting me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How did you recognise their voices?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I recognised their voices because I knew the gentlemen, personally. I'd had several occasions to meet up with them and talk to them, so I did not have any doubt when I recognised Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Stanisic's voices.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in this -- for these purposes, we'll just look at the transcript of the conversation. But without referring to a specific page, perhaps I could ask you this question: Having reviewed -- having listened to the conversation and reviewed the transcript, does this conversation have any relationship with the meeting described in paragraph 69 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the conversation took place one day after the meeting at Ilidza. And from this conversation, it transpires from Mr. Jovanovic attended that meeting, and he -- or, rather, Mr. Stanisic attended that meeting and shared his impression with Mr. Jovanovic. In other words, they are commenting the meeting that had taken place in Ilidza one day before, and the topic of that conversation were the governing bodies of the SDS, where they were going to function, whether it would be in Pale or whether they would be moved to Ilidza. In other words, the immediate cause for that conversation was the meeting that had taken place at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we can go over. And since you can read English perfectly, Mr. Kezunovic, I wonder if we can remove the Serbian version of the transcript from the screen. If we can go over to page 2 of this transcript, I see Mr. Stanisic saying, towards the bottom of the page -- sorry, go back to the preceding page. My mistake, page 1 of the transcript. Mr. Stanisic says he was at a meeting at Ilidza until midnight the previous day, at the bottom of the page. And now if you move over to page 2, he says: "Everyone was there, including the Crisis Staff of Ilidza. The big boss held the meeting." And later in the transcript, at page 4, he says Krajisnik was there, Momo Pejic was there, Nadazdin was there and Simovic were there. Does that correspond with your recollection of the attendees at page 69 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Milivoj Nadazdin is the name. He was the minister of agriculture in the government of the then Bosnia and Herzegovina. Pejic, Simovic, were also member of the government on behalf of the SDS. Mr. Miodrag Simovic was the vice-president of that government as well. And as far as I can remember, there were eight members of the then government present at the meeting, and they were all representatives of the SDS in the then government of Jure Pelivan. In other words, eight ministers were present that evening. In addition to the three you mentioned, there were others. I wouldn't mention all of their names; I'm afraid I might make a mistake. But there were eight of them present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also in this conversation, at pages 4 and 6, Jovo Jovanovic says: "I didn't convene the Crisis Staff. I have no people." And, further: "I didn't put this staff of mine into operation. I practically surrendered. I'm not doing anything. I didn't activate you because there was no need," because he practically took over the command and is running the municipality directly. Now, given this, I wonder if you see any relationship between this conversation and the document mentioned in paragraphs 51 and 52 of your statement, 65 ter 08176, listing the membership of the Crisis Staff for Sarajevo, dated 24 December 1991. And you will recall that document lists --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Jovo Jovanovic and Stanisic as members.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 08176.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see in front of you a document dated 24 December 1991, listing the members of the Crisis Staff for the Serbian Democratic Party for the city of Sarajevo, with Jovo Jovanovic and Maksim Stanisic under numbers 1 and 2 among the members?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, seeing this document, do you see any relationship between the intercepted conversation of 19 April and this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this document, you can see that previously we were talking about the Crisis Staff in the territory of Ilidza, and the document that we can see in front of us shows the composition of the Crisis Staff for the city of Sarajevo. And let me remind you that Sarajevo had 10 municipalities, and Ilidza was just one of them. There was a crisis staff for Sarajevo, just as there were crisis staffs for all the 10 municipalities. And the intercepted conversation describes the situation or the drastic differences, in terms of the organisation and functioning of the Crisis Staff in Ilidza that is functioning, that pursues activities, it was established, whereas it transpires from Mr. Jovo Jovanovic's statement that the Crisis Staff does not function in Sarajevo at all. And as we could hear from this conversation, Mr. Jovo Jovanovic says that the Crisis Staff did not pursue any activities, that it couldn't, nor did he intend to launch the activities of the Crisis Staff. As far as I can remember, the Crisis Staff for the city of Sarajevo actually never took off the ground, never started functioning properly. So there is a direct link between the intercepted conversation and the document that is currently in front of us on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Finally, can we please go back to the intercepted conversation -- the transcript of the intercepted conversation, with one last question. That's 30682. If we could go to page 8 of the English. 30682, page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, about halfway down that page, you see Mr. Jovanovic saying --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Can this be blown up just a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see Mr. Jovanovic saying, about halfway down that page: "We ought to negotiate in the town to continue to exist and function." And then Maksim Stanisic says, immediately following: "Let me tell you something. This is a matter for the republic organs because it's the capital. But their insistence on the division of Sarajevo and the drawing of maps ..." And I wonder if you have any comment on this last --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do have a comment. I can see that we have to establish a certain context. Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Jovanovic were the two most prominent people in the city of Sarajevo. Jovo Jovanovic was the first president of the city Board of the SDS and Mr. Maksim Stanisic, who was the president of the Executive Board of the city of Sarajevo on behalf of the SDS, and the two number-one men, as it were, who were members of the administration and in these institutions of government. And the party had dilemmas about their own roles and about their own functioning, when it came to the work that they were supposed to do in Sarajevo, and it is very clear from their conversation that their positions were identical to mine, and that was that efforts had to be made to talk with the partners in the government between the parties in order to reach an agreement that would be put in place while a final solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina and Sarajevo were being sought. And when it comes to decision -- divisions in Sarajevo, we have to note that there were a lot of pressures coming from the municipalities in Sarajevo because of inter-ethnic conflicts and the skirmishes that happened on the ground. They wanted to achieve some sort of reorganisation or territorial reshaping of Sarajevo, and that's why Mr. Stanisic says "drawing of the maps." There were ideas to try and find solution in that way. But both Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Stanisic thought that that would have been a wrong way, and I agreed with them, which means that we were like-minded at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be marked for further identification, according to the usual practices, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P2528, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, still in relation to paragraph 69 of your statement, you said that in mid-April, the Serb leaders left the Holiday Inn and moved to the Hotel Srbija in Ilidza. Koljevic was there; Karadzic and Krajisnik came from time to time. My question is quite simple: If Karadzic and Krajisnik were there from time to time, where were they the rest of the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can answer in general terms, from what I remember. Both Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik worked at the Holiday Inn, up to a dramatic event when the hotel was surrounded, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, I've referred you to the paragraph that says: "In mid-April, the Serb leaders left the Holiday Inn and moved to the Hotel Srbija in Ilidza. "... Koljevic was there. Karadzic and Krajisnik came from time to time." Do you know where Karadzic and Krajisnik were the rest of the time they weren't in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that they were in Pale. But we're talking about the meeting that took place on that day, and of course, Mr. Koljevic spent longer times in Ilidza, where he worked from the Srbija Hotel, and on that day, when that meeting took place, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik also came. Mr. Stanisic attended, I attended, and all of us from Ilidza, and that was a huge gathering at which we decided where the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be working from then on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. On paragraph 74 of your statement, you said on one occasion in mid-May, you saw paramilitaries coming to Ilidza on buses from Drina, Zvornik. Apart from that one occasion, do you have any other information on paramilitary forces in the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything about information. I can tell you what I experienced with my own eyes. When I abandoned all of my formal positions, I continued living in Ilidza, and at that time Ilidza was a very small municipality and all of us knew each other very well. When somebody new turned up, we all noticed that. At that time, people, wearing different uniforms unknown to us appeared in larger numbers. I'm talking about May and June. People arrived in Ilidza whom we today call paramilitary formations. I don't know what they were called at the time. Let me share a concrete example. It was not Drina-Zvornik, but it was a bus owned by the Drinatrans company from Zvornik, and it carried uniformed people. That happened over one weekend. They spent the entire weekend there. They participated in some actions in Ilidza municipality, I suppose. What I remember is that those same men got on the same bus and left Ilidza, but that bus was full of stolen goods; and not only the bus, but there were also passenger vehicles full of the looted goods that they had stolen in Ilidza. That was their weekend warfare, as it were. I was not very pleased, and that was not an only example. There were several occasions when people in uniforms arrived, ostensibly to help the Serbs in Ilidza, but actually why they came was to loot what they could. They actually made use of our war drama in Ilidza to gain their own benefit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say "different uniforms," as you did in one of your answers, what did you mean? What was different about those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, they were varied, there were all sorts of uniforms, ranging from the uniforms of the former Territorial Defence, to camouflage uniforms of the JNA, the police uniforms of all shades of blue or white. They mostly came in groups of 10 to 15 men, and those groups did have identical uniforms, and they had some insignia showing affiliation to one of those paramilitary formations. These were all characteristics of the initial period in May/June when chaos reigned supreme in Ilidza. Later on, when the structure of police and the police organs started being established, and when the Army of Republika Srpska took over and organised themselves as a military, those paramilitary formations dwindled in numbers and finally completely disappeared from our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go back to my question and focus on the uniforms, as I was doing. I'll just revert to one of your answers, actually. You said they had groups: "They had some insignia showing some affiliation to one of those paramilitary formations." Do you remember those, in particular? And if so, what were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. They were small groups, and they all had insignia, but none of them known to me. And to be honest, my experiences of seeing them were very short, so I wouldn't be able to remember them. Some of them just wore bands around their sleeves, which allowed them to recognise themselves as belonging to the same group. So, unfortunately, I wouldn't be able to tell you who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember the presence of a group under the control of a man named Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that Brne Gavrilovic's name is well known. I know that a group of Brne Gavrilovic's Chetniks arrived in Ilidza sometime in the summer of 1992, which is beyond the scope of the period to which I'm testifying. Brne Gavrilovic's group was in Ilidza as of summer 1992. However, from the 15th of May, I did not hold any formal position in Ilidza, but I can confirm that Mr. Brne Gavrilovic's group was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, similarly, the names of any other commanders of these groups that you've been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that at that time, I didn't know any of the names. I only saw those groups of people coming and going and passing through. Later on, subsequently, I learned who they were. I didn't know at the time, but later on, in conversations, in following trials, in talking to people in Ilidza, I learned their names were Legija - he was there with a group - and then there was Bokan. Again, I don't know his full name, and he was there with his group for a short period of time. They would arrive for weekends or they would spend seven or ten days in Ilidza. In general terms, Seselj's men would come from Zvornik. They were referred to as Seselj's men. I don't know whether they were a member of Seselj's party or his formation, but they were popularly known as Seselj's men. And they also came, they spent a short time in Ilidza, and then they left. Seselj, himself, also spent some time in Ilidza. I wasn't there, but Mr. Nedjo Prstojevic, in a conversation, told me that he had spoken with him, that he had met up with him, and that Seselj had also visited Ilidza together with Mr. Tomislav Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have one last question in your examination-in-chief, and it relates to paragraph 72 of your statement. There, you indicated that civilians in the Serbian municipality of Ilidza had the same as the civilians of Sarajevo. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean by "they had the same"? What do you mean? If you mean -- oh, right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your statement, you said --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 72. Yes, I can answer, yes. I spent the entire war at Ilidza. Ilidza was divided into east and west parts, and in the middle was Hrasnica. That was under the control of the Bosniak Muslim forces. When I was not in the western part, where I resided, I was in the eastern part, where I worked in the Famos company, and I witnessed all the war developments that took place at Ilidza throughout the war, and especially those events that were described by the victims of the misfortune that we experienced at Ilidza, as its residents. I, as a resident of Ilidza, can say that in my immediate vicinity, I saw the killings, the sniping, the artillery shells falling all over Ilidza. A drastic example would be the example of a child, who was my son's friend, a 13-year-old boy, Bojan Stijak, who was killed by a sniper. My first-door neighbour, Katica, who was a Croat, was injured by a shell that had been launched from Hrasnica. My acquaintance and friend, Drasko Vukosav, a member of the government, was also a victim of the events in Ilidza. And my overall assessment was that when it came to the war at Ilidza and the general situation at Ilidza, I compared all that with the situation in Sarajevo that was encircled, and my assessment was that the population of Ilidza was in an identical position, that they were exposed to sniping, artillery fire, and there were a lot of victims and casualties. I witnessed a lot of those events. I barely survived some of those events myself. And the number of victims, in contrast with the small area of Ilidza, which had about 30.000 inhabitants at the time, I can tell you that over a thousand were killed. They were elderly, children, women. In public spaces, they were killed. And the overall situation in Ilidza was almost identical to the situation that prevailed in Sarajevo that was under siege. And this is what I tried to describe in paragraph 72. I tried to describe the situation at Ilidza and how the citizens of Ilidza, the combatants, the civilians, how they fared through the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention for the transcript, if I may. The witness said that the situation in Sarajevo was something that he knew from the video. Very important, and it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is very important. I wasn't in Sarajevo at the time. I was near Sarajevo, about a hundred metres away from Sarajevo, because there was a border, as it were, between Sarajevo and Ilidza. I can talk about Sarajevo only based on what I heard and saw in the media. Apart from that, I can say that I personally survived --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say video, I said media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the witness is continuing to answer the question that you asked, but -- and is now, as it were, making the addition as to the video which was interjected, and I think properly interjected by Dr. Karadzic, because it didn't appear in the transcript. Was that the end of your questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, that's the end of the questions of the Office of the Prosecutor. We're now going to turn to the cross-examination from Dr. Karadzic, but we're going to do that after the break which we will take between now and 11.00. But can I ask you this -- to do this: There are time constraints. It's not a criticism, but you are plainly a voluble witness who -- it's plain that you're an intelligent and thoughtful man, but you must, please, try, first of all, to answer the actual question which has been asked with as much exactitude as possible and, secondly, to be as concise as an accurate answer allows. Dr. Karadzic is also under time constraints, and it's only fair to him to do that. So until 11.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, if I may, there's a short matter of a small number of associated exhibits to deal with that I omitted to deal with before we broke. And those associated exhibits referred to in the amalgamated statement, that I would now move to tender as Prosecution exhibits, have 65 ter numbers 16198, 10825, 16200, 08176, 17237, and the last, 30607, which I would be asked to be marked for identification as it is a transcript of an intercepted telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. Then, those will be so admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, they will be Exhibit P2529 through P2533.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kezunovic. Right at the outset, I want to express my gratitude to you for meeting with the Defence, so I hope that these three hours will enable us to shed light on the greatest part of your testimony, if not all. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you: Did you provide a supplemental sheet to the Prosecution over the past two days, including 20 paragraphs or 20 bullet points? We discussed it yesterday. Can we call -- can we call 1D3520. Do you recall providing that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spent two days with the Prosecution in proofing, and I just clarified some of my statements given, beginning 2004, to date. It just clarified what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3520 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: As I've said, I haven't seen it. What I had before me and have before me still is the amalgamated statement. I haven't seen this text before, but I believe it reflects what I've discussed with the Prosecution over the past two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in response to questions from the Prosecution, in this statement you clarified some points from the amalgamated statements?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the Defence offer this document too?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness hasn't seen it. He said two times that he hasn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that does make it rather difficult, Dr. Karadzic. Hold on to it for the moment. There may be another way in which you can produce it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we could ask the witness to look at the document during the break and authorise it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, it's all right, I accept it. It's up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is this proposal acceptable, that the witness look at the document during the break to see if it reflects, indeed, his positions, and then it could be admitted, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the witness has said he accepts it, without having seen it, which perhaps is a little less than satisfactory. So it would be better if the witness does see the document, and then the determination can be made when he's been able to refresh his memory or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, any objections to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, not at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you to clear up a little the tensions in Ilidza in 1990, before the elections and concerning the elections. Do you agree that these tensions did not originate in Ilidza, they were just a reflection of overall tensions in Yugoslavia that arose with the appearance of new political forces in Slovenia and Croatia, and the first indications that Yugoslavia might be broken up?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can hardly connect Ilidza and the events in Ilidza with the global level of political events in Yugoslavia at the time. What is specific to Ilidza and what I can discuss is an analogy -- a parallel between Ilidza and the Yugoslavia as it was then in the 1990s. And this similarity lies in the fact that Bosnia was Yugoslavia, in a nutshell, and Sarajevo was again a nutshell of Yugoslavia at a lower level, and Ilidza was, in terms of its structure, very consistent with the structure of 1990s Yugoslavia. So all the disagreements that existed at the time in Yugoslavia were very quickly felt in Ilidza because of its ethnic structure, which reflected the ethnic structure of Bosnia and of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope you understand I have to make a pause between your answers and my questions to enable the interpreters to do their job. So there was nothing that happened in Ilidza to generate these tensions. On the contrary, the tensions in Ilidza were the result of overall developments in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember anything from those times, any single event that happened in Ilidza or a disagreement that contributed to tensions in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Esteemed Ms. Edgerton showed a video here which we won't show again - there's no need - but it shows St. George's Feast which, in your view, resulted in a protest of taxi-drivers in Ilidza and the surrounding area. I'm not sure if it's quite clear to the Chamber. Is it the case that those taxi-drivers were Muslims from Sarajevo who demonstratively passed through Serbian areas?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say what I haven't seen myself. There was a motorcade of vehicles, and they were taxis. Who the drivers were, I didn't know, but I heard the shouts from those cars. I could distinguish what they were saying. I heard the volleys of gun-fire on the bridge in Ilidza, and all of us who were there think that it was a protest, a demonstration of the Muslim structures in Sarajevo against the presence of Vojislav Seselj at this St. George's Feast Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Judging by the shouts, what they were saying, could you identify or determine who they were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was quite clear who was protesting and on whose behalf they were saying, "The Chetniks will not pass," "Sarajevo is a place where there's no room for Chetniks." Nobody said they were Muslims, but it was quite clear from their words on behalf of which part of Sarajevo they were saying these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'll ask you to answer with a yes or no, if possible. Can we agree that Novakova Cave is an old locality mentioned in our epic poetry, and it's about 70 kilometres from Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I am from Ilidza, and I was born not far from that Novakova Cave. Yes, you're right. It's actually 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that meeting in Novakova Cave was in a completely uninhabited area, a place normally used for picnics?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Novakova Cave is a rather famous tourist site near Sarajevo where people go very often and where people traditionally gathered on St. George's Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it was not a populated area? There were no Muslims who could be offended by that gathering, that holiday?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was born not far from Mount Romanija, Novakova Cave is linked to the brigands from Ottoman times in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as far as nearby villages are concerned, the first village is Careve Vode, where the population is half-half, Serbs and Muslims. All of them are my neighbours. But from what I remember of those times, there were no disagreements or protests from that village against the gathering of St. George's Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said it was a tradition. Let me remind you. Do you agree that the tradition of early-morning gatherings on St. George's Day is something that exists for centuries, attended by Muslims and Serbs and especially the Roma of all religions? Is that a century-old holiday or something that we introduced in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: You're completely right. It's a tradition respected by everyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially the Roma, Serbs and Muslims. It's an old tradition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, could we look at 65 ter 30487 -- sorry, 478, 65 ter 30478, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that Mr. Seselj was also in that video, and at that time he still did not have a party, he only had the Chetnik movement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't confirm or deny, because at that time I wasn't following these things, and I don't know whether the party of Mr. Vojislav Seselj existed. As for him being in that video, yes, he was there. I saw that after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In any case, he wasn't in power in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2 of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom, in English it straddles pages 3 and 4. We see Tintor is talking to me, and I say -- I'll read it to you in our language. Tintor says: "Okay. I asked him not to deal with this, and Seselj, he was at the Assembly." And Karadzic says: "Yes. Somebody else should do that from his staff. These staffs are no good. They shouldn't be dealing with that. That's up to the army." And then there's some profanity, and then Karadzic says: "What do Seselj's soldiers have to do with it? They should go to the army." That is in December, before the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot testify about this, either the transcript or the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this position that I took, that there should be no troops except those who are formally part of the army, do you know that it was consistent with my overall position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard many of your statements in this context, and it's consistent with what you are saying here. I've had occasion to hear that in your earlier statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was me and the SDS, as a whole, and even the authorities in which the SDS took part, were always emphatically against any military formations, apart from the army?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I said that in my previous answer. What I heard in your earlier statements is consistent with that. That's what I recall. I remember you publicly expressed that position at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I'm advised that, in fact, it can be admitted, rather than MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, based on the view that there is a translation in place. However, based on our position in relation to the pre-war intercepts having been made on an unlawful basis, we are seeking that it be admitted as MFI'd only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I mean, your position as to that has been made plain. The fact -- the difference between MFI'ing and admitting has no qualitative difference as to how it's taken into account by the Trial Chamber. It's only a question of technicality. So I don't think you're going to lose your position simply by having it admitted now, but it saves it forming part of the enormous bundle of material that would otherwise need further translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1251, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to clarify something, for the sake of the Chamber and everyone involved, the issue concerning illegal housing developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about people moving in from Sandzak, you're referring to what were mostly Muslims coming to Sarajevo to -- I think 99 per cent of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that Sokolovic Kolonija was built in a stretch of Ilidza which was made up of Serbian neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: One of the problems that were there, objectively, when it comes to the settling of population in Ilidza, was that this was an area that traditionally belonged to the Serbs. However, it is also true that land was not taken forcibly; it was bought off Serbs by individuals arriving from Sandzak. However, the structures built on that land did not have the requisite building permits, and they did not pay for any of the infrastructure costs involved, municipal levies normally imposed on that sort of land, et cetera. So these were basically illegal structures, and the problem was that there was a whole lot of them. It was a large quantity of such structures, in the context of Ilidza as a small place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Sanac, Sokoljevo, or that is to say, Sokolovic Kolonija, Buca Potok?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that all these illegal neighbourhoods emerged in what were traditionally Serb areas or, rather, Serb land?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same applies to Sokolovic Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that we distinguish in our language between increasing population and natural increase? When we talk about natural increase, that is through birth, and increase in general is through other deliberate or just natural ways in which it happens?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness answers immediately after Dr. Karadzic finishes his question, and I wonder if he could just be encouraged to make just even a brief pause to allow our colleagues to catch up to ensure we have the most accurate transcript possible.
