utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. When you're both speaking the same language fluently, it's very easy to engage in a conversation, as opposed to a question and answer. The translators do a great job, but can you assist them by slowing it down a bit, please, and putting a pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to all. I apologise to the Trial Chamber. It was an oversight on my part. It will not happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One other question. Do you agree that there existed three reasons for the artificial increase in population that were generally known; the settling of people from Sandzak; the thesis that there were four million Bosniaks and three million of their descendants in Turkey; and, lastly, that the top religious cleric issued the instruction that the Muslims should have at least five children in a family to secure the independence of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Where you mentioned the settling of people from Sandzak, this was a matter of fact that was obvious for everyone to see. It had been going on from the 1970s all the way to the 1990s, the beginning of the war. As for the other issues you mentioned, the possible settlement of Bosniaks from Turkey, yes, I do recall such and other similar statements by Mr. Ceric, the top cleric, that all the Turks -- or that's to say all the individuals who left the Balkans after the Balkan wars in 1912, were, in fact, leaving together with many Bosniaks. These Bosniaks were now Turkish citizens, and the number mentioned at the time was seven million Bosniaks who were citizens of Turkey and who claimed that Bosnia-Herzegovina was their country of origin and their domicile. And they were announcing the possibility of all these individuals returning, but nothing has come out of that. If we look back at the 1990s, all the way to this day, nothing has been seen of this announced return of Turkish Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now call up 65 ter 22142. This is your statement, dated the 30th of January, 2008. I'd like to ask you about your views of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear, can I ask you to confirm, if you can, briefly, please, that you had never been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true, but if I can be allowed to explain this in one sentence. People who showed up at my door-step in 1990 to -- asking me to be on the SDS list, had they insisted that I become a member of the SDS, I would have done so. But there was no such insistence, so it so happened that I never joined the SDS at the time. And the situation prevailed in that same way to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the individuals who set up the Serbian Democratic Party had for decades been dissidents or some sort of an opposition and that they did not have -- they were not endowed with the abilities to run the government, to run the state, and that was the reason why they placed professionals, people with the requisite expertise who were not members of the party, on their list?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of many individuals who, at the time when the SDS was in the making, and that was in 1990, were invited by the SDS to take up a number of significant positions, from the municipal all the way up to the republican level, without having been members of the SDS. In the main, these were competent individuals who were able to professionally carry out the duties they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that as you were forming the municipal government, you asked for a free hand to be able to include in the Municipal Board people of high qualities, rather than political suitability?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask that the Executive Board, that is to say the local government, be made up of people that I proposed, who did not necessarily have to be members of the SDS. At the same time, this was only true of the SDS. The other two parties, the SDA and HDZ, insisted that only those who were members of their respective parties could have been nominated for any of the functions within the local government.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have page 3 of the document, item 11 -- paragraph 11. I'd like to read it out: "The purpose of the Main Board was to carry out the political goals of the party, just like any political party. The Main Board set policy and fulfilled the intentions stated in the party's documents, expressed as political intentions, intentions with regard to resolving the problems of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that when it came to issues of human resources, the resolution of problems locally, the local level of the SDS had full autonomy and freedom in their activity?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the illustration I gave was the Executive Board of the Municipality of Ilidza, where, at my insistence, people who were not members of any political party were asked to join. Mr. Salovic [phoen] and Ms. Snjezana Soldat [phoen] were the individuals who performed certain duties within the municipality even in the previous period during the socialist times, and I decided to keep them in their jobs during my term of office there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it was a matter of general knowledge that it is the Main Board that is in charge of running a certain political party, and not an individual?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I did say as much. That was my understanding of how the party worked, and that was a fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 949, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that's now P2529, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This will make it easier for us. We don't have to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at the document, specifically at the preamble, which reads: "It is a well-known general recommendation of the Serbian Democratic Party of BiH that the principal place for the party's activity should be the local board. Because of the risk that the party's bureaucratisation and self-congratulatory isolation within a circle of the party's officials separated from the people, the president from the SDS issued the following:" Et cetera. Can you help the Trial Chamber understand what the local board and the local commune stand for? Is that the lowest structure of organisation that would exist in a village? Is that the basic structure which helps a certain neighbourhood resolve its day-to-day problems?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right about that. The municipality of Ilidza had 19 local communes, Blazuj, Centre of Ilidza, Vojkovici, Hrasnica, Grlica, Kasindol, et cetera. There were 19 local communes in all, which were basic structures of organisation. They had their own organs of self-government which saw to it that life in general was running smoothly. In other words, the local commune was the basic unit of administrative structure of every municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including that of Ilidza. All the political parties had their own political structure at the level of the local commune so that every party had its local board at the level of the local commune, including the SDS. And in most of these local boards - not all of them, but most of them - had not only the local self-government unit, but also the party local commune. And then higher up from there, you would have the Municipal Board, and higher up the Town Board, et cetera. But in that structure, the lowest level of organisation was the local board within a local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that the position of the SDS was that that was the place where the party had to pursue its activities, and not higher up?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, because that was the level where people lived, had day-to-day problems, and that was the level where they had to be -- where it had to be resolved, in the grassroots. And that was not only the case in that period, because the local Communist unit of organisation existed in the previous times as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't think that this has been admitted. Let me ask you this: Would you say that this is the position on the maxim of "decentralisation of power"?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Objectively speaking, the only presentation or the only characteristic of the party's democratic nature was that it functions from the grassroots, from the local communes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Has this been admitted? If so, then we don't have a problem with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to draw your attention to the phenomenon of regionalisation. Can one say that you were more familiar with the idea of administrative or regionalisation of urban areas, especially Sarajevo, than with the creation of regions around Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't talk about Serbian autonomous provinces because I was not involved in those activities. However, when it comes to the ideas that dealt with the territorial and administrative reconstruction of the city of Sarajevo, I was very much involved in that, so my answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the prewar appearance -- or, rather, the administrative appearance of the city of Sarajevo, with 10 municipalities, was not always the same, that there were changes, that there were municipalities such as, for example, Pazaric, Blazuj, Rajlovac, and that our administrative reconstruction of Sarajevo would not have been the first one, but, rather, that such reconstructions had happened even before that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Let's not go far back, but let's say that after the Second World War, the administrative organisation of the city of Sarajevo relied on the so-called districts, and then that administrative form was abandoned and gave place to another administrative and territorial organisation at the level of the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, the borders of the administrative units, which were known as municipalities, were changed. And in practical terms, from the Second World War to the 1990s of the last century, there were constant attempts to reorganise the territory with a view to meet the interests of the grassroots of the local communes. So this was an ongoing process. The territorial reorganisation of Sarajevo was an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it comes to local communes, did they have the constitutional right to vote in referendums on leaving one municipality and joining another municipality? Did the municipality have the right to join a different association of municipalities by leaving their previous ones?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the association of municipalities, this was not a new term, this was not a newly-coined term. That existed during the socialist times of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it still exists. Local communes in the previous period were legal subjects. They were organisations that were organised by the population in a smaller area, and based on the laws of the then Bosnia-Herzegovina, they had the right to be consulted on any issue that concerned their rights stemming from that territory, and that included referendums, joining another municipality, changes in administrative and territorial borders. What applied to local communes also applied to municipalities in general. At the end of the day, I can say, since I was very much involved in local self-government, I can say that this is a process that exists, that is guaranteed by the European Charter on Local Self-government, which guarantees all local communes in all the 47 states of the European Council to have autonomy on decision-making or processes concerning decisions on issues important for that local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe the Trial Chamber and the participants in these proceedings are not very clear on the distributive role and nature of socialism. Let me ask you: Was it advantageous for a municipality, which held the seats of the regions or the seats of chambers of commerce, which means that the payment institutions were there, does it mean that those places which were regional centres developed much faster than all the other places within that region?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness has already answered the question, because both Dr. Karadzic and the witness are speaking with great speed and alacrity. But I was rising, Your Honour, because that's not an appropriate question for this witness, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it demands a level of expertise which this witness may or may not have, but, in any event, it may not be an area of evidence that is going to be very useful. I speak for myself when I say that. Can we move on, gentlemen, and again may I exhort you please to remember the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question, then. Is it true that, for example, the municipalities that disappeared in Sarajevo, such as Blazuj or Rajlovac, stopped developing, and that that development had long-term consequences on their development?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Not only Blazuj and Rajlovac. It is a fact that was valid throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. Where administration was focused in any sense, that municipality developed faster than all the other towns which did not hold centres of administration. This was a fact that was true of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but in all of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was prompted by this: In the indictment, it is suggested that our intentions on regionalisation or administrative redistribution had a political nature. It is the Defence case that even before the break-up of Yugoslavia, such measures were governed by economic reasons, because municipalities that lost their position as seats of administrative government lagged in development?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused be kindly asked to make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was rising for the same reason that my colleagues in the booth have just spoken up. It's absolutely impossible to follow the conversation between these two gentlemen unless they slow down, for all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I don't have to ask twice. I shall ask for a third and, I hope, for the last time. Put a pause between questions and answers, please, a conscious pause, and please speak more slowly. It's difficult, I know, to speak at a pace less than one's natural pace of speaking, but it's very important that you do so when it's being interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I am under the pressure of time, but still I will try to make those pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this: As the president of the municipal government, with your colleague, who was the president of the municipal parliament, who was a Muslim, a representative of the SDA, you managed to preserve order in Ilidza, although you were privy to the information that the Muslim community had established a military organisation, the so-called Patriotic League; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: There are two questions in one. The first one, whether Mr. Mahmutovic and I tried, during the period from February to April 1992, to postpone the expressions of conflict in Ilidza, and the answer to that would be yes, I can confirm this, and I'm sure that Mr. Mahmutovic can confirm this. He was the then number-one man in the then municipality of Ilidza. He was the president of its parliament. Mr. Mahmutovic and myself agreed on most things. We would give ourselves tasks or the task to preserve Ilidza, to protect it until the final solution is reached for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we did that in co-operation with the then existing police structure in Ilidza, headed by Edin Lidic and Tomo Kovac. Our intention was successfully realised. In order to do that, there had to be mutual trust between the two of us. We had to be convinced that we were involved in something that was for the benefit of all our citizens. In order to gain mutual trust, we also had to exchange information on the situation and the events that took place in Ilidza at that time. That's how I was informed about the second part of your question, and that is that the entire municipality of Ilidza was being armed -- or, rather, that Bosniak Muslims were being armed. I received information that the Patriotic League had, indeed, been organised, and so on and so forth. So the answer to both parts of your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether the Serb structures in the government were under the pressure of Serbs who felt threatened by the Patriotic League, by the influx of refugees from Croatia, and so on and so forth? Were people under pressure and distressed, and did they request protection from the bodies of authority? Did they ask you to allow them to organise themselves in a similar manner?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we go back to the year 1992, to the spring of 1992, and if we briefly remember the context which saw the end to the war in Croatia, and if we remember that we had a lot of refugees who had arrived in Ilidza from Croatia and who wanted to find solution to their problems, we have to remember that there was an overall atmosphere of fear in expectation as to what would happen to all of us in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I, personally, and all of us in Ilidza, were under pressure from all the other municipalities and their populations to try and find a solution to stop the spiral of misfortune that was in place, for the course of events to be turned around, and to avoid the destiny of our neighbours in Croatia. The pressure was put on us by the general population, who wanted us to find a political solution in order to prevent the happenings that loomed upon us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would kindly ask you to look at the document known as Variants A and B. You have already said something about that document in your statement. Could you please tell us whether it is correct that the meeting which took place on the 19th December 1991 was a very big meeting, involving some 400 or 500 people at Holiday Inn Hotel, and that among the attendees were members of the Main Board, the representatives of the government, the presidents of the municipal boards from the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina? In other words, was that a very public and a very large-scale meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I attended that meeting on the 19th of December, 1991. It was a large gathering, as you said it yourself. Anybody who held a public position on behalf of the SDS from all over Bosnia and Herzegovina were present at that meeting. I remember that meeting very well. I remember the hall where it took place. I would say that your figure of 400 attendees is quite an objective figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that this paper was distributed outside of the agenda of the meeting, that no discussion preceded the adoption of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already told you that I remember the meeting very well. I remember the topics very well. I remember individuals who took the floor, for example, Bozidar Vucurevic. I still remember some of the sentences he uttered on that occasion. I remember that it was a meeting which analysed the current political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in late 1991. During the course of the meeting, nobody said anything about any variants, either A or B. Nobody announced during the meeting that materials would be distributed during the meeting, nor, indeed, were materials distributed in written or any other form. The material under that name, Variant A and B, is something that I saw for the first time during my interview with the OTP in 2004. However, even before that, in early January 1992, I heard of the existence of such a document. However, I never saw it with my own two eyes before the Prosecutor showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was not imposed on you, as president of the local government, as an obligation or a document that you should act upon, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, you probably saw or read that this paper, although we're not now discussing who created it, that this paper also envisaged care for citizens of other ethnic groups and religions and their inclusion in the administration. But when you saw that document, did you think that it had some military wisdom to it, a military effort to prevent some undesirable developments? Did you see the old Communist mentality in that paper?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it would be inappropriate for me to comment on a document that I saw five or six years after it was created. I believe it would be wisdom in hindsight, but, yes, I did have the impression when I saw it that it was driven by a logic of the previous system.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call a map of Ilidza. It's this binder, ERN 0701-0751. It's Map 30 in this binder. I don't know the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, then, that Ilidza municipality did not always look this way, that it looked a bit different when Rajlovac municipality existed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19129 is the 65 ter number. Is that right, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering how the witness was able to answer that question when none of us seem to have the map on the screen in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe the witness knows his municipality well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, frankly, Your Honour, I don't know the 65 ter number of the map Dr. Karadzic proposes to use, because we weren't notified he was going to use a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's the inscrutable workings of providence, Ms. Edgerton. But let's have the map on the screen, and the witness can be asked if his answer accords with the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my previous answer, I didn't comment on a map which I didn't see, but it's a fact that Ilidza municipality changed with time in its administrative borders and outlook. We'll now look at the map and see what it's like.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19108 is the right number. I apologise. Now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a map of Ilidza municipality, and is it a bit elongated like a lizard?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is elongated. Whether it's lizard-shaped, I wouldn't know. Yes, it's typical. It stretches quite long, and that's what I spoke about in my previous answers to the Prosecution, the territorial appearance of Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the central part, but not too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then I would ask you to take a pen that would be activated by the Usher, and mark for the Trial Chamber predominantly Serb and predominantly Muslim and predominantly Croat areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: At what point in history, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Current. I believe this is a pre-war map. 1991, 1992, early 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hrasnica was traditionally predominantly Muslim. That's the area in brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you put a circle around predominantly Muslim neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid you also included Otes and Stup. Can you erase this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to erase it. Is that possible? Hrasnica is only this part here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you now focus. You see Donji Kotorac, Gornji Kotorac, Vojkovici, Sokolovic Kolonija, airport, Ilidza, Stup, Otes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's easier to enumerate. Sokolovic Kolonija, as I already said [marks]. This part of Ilidza is practically the centre, where the population was very mixed [marks]. Otes and Stup were parts of Ilidza with predominantly Croat population, including Bare, that we see to the north. As for the rest of Ilidza, Hrasnica, of course, I mentioned it as predominantly Muslim. And the rest to the right, Vojkovici, Donje Mladice, Kasindol, that's predominantly Serb. Blazuj is also predominantly Serb. And territorially speaking, all these areas were very concentrated. Osijek was totally Serb, densely concentrated in one area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you one thing. Do you agree that there was talk about establishing two municipalities, one Serbian and one Muslim, and there was talk about creating a Croat municipality? Can you show us what they would look like? Were they consistent with the front-line? Was the Muslim municipality supposed to include Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir, Hrasnica, and Donji Kotorac?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It must have been one of the discussions about territorial divisions. None of these options was ever finalised, in terms of an agreement. Those were all possibilities on the table, but they were never completely agreed to by all the three ethnic groups. Those were options proposed by one or another ethnic community, depending on their interests. One was Serbian, Bosniak, and the third Croat, but all of them boiled down to the proposal that the Bosniak part was to have its seat in Hrasnica, the Croat around Stup, and the Serbian one around Vojkovici and Kasindol. Those were three areas of Ilidza that were ethnically compact and mostly ethnically balanced. That was supposed to be the territorial division, but it was never finalised. There was never a consensus about them, never an agreement, so none of them was ever verified. Those were a series of ideas about territorial restructuring of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked this because I want to see whether this is consistent with territories controlled by Muslims, by Serbs and by Croats, respectively.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Serbs and Croats try to take control of those areas of Ilidza that were controlled by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of the war and the beginning of hostilities was right at the outset, and the separating lines were along these divisions in Ilidza. In Stup, we had the centre of HVO, and part of Stup was controlled by Croatian forces. Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija and this part of Butmir, up to the airport, was an area controlled by Bosniak Muslim forces. And to the east and west, those separated parts of Ilidza were under the control of Serbian forces, and that was established as a separation line according to those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't have to draw that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's quite clear from this map, these territorial divisions within Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you now if it is true that one needs to make a distinction between the establishment of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Ilidza and the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza? Is it the case that the Serbian Assembly in Ilidza was a kind of house, like house of the people, not a national assembly that was established in 1992, early 1992, not as a territory; it was functionally like a house of the people, the kind we have now. Do you agree that there is a distinction between the Assembly of the Serbian People in Ilidza and the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza that was set up later?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have already discussed that it was on the 3rd of January, 1992, that the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza, it was a political act of the Serbian Democratic Party. It was practically an institution that never really came to life, never really worked, because I was president of that assembly and I never convened a single assembly session. I never sent out a single invitation, and that assembly never convened. However, in the beginning of April, this second assembly was formed, the one you mentioned. It began to work in early April, the beginning of hostilities in Ilidza, and it operated the way you described. Those were two different assemblies that worked in completely different ways but also in completely different circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To clear up the terminology, can we see 65 ter 16200. There's also a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Before we do that, Dr. Karadzic, what do you want in respect of this map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing, Your Excellency, because nothing is marked on it. I just wanted to see, the Trial Chamber, what the distribution of neighbourhoods is. Although you've seen it before, but you can see it here on a map, they are practically clearly defined, except the centre. All the rest is Muslim or Serb or Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Very well. By looking at the map and the transcript, that becomes obvious. There is no need, as you say, to admit the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 16200.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's now P2531, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the headline, the journalists combined my name and your surname. It says on the 11th of January, in the famous tourist spot in Ilidza municipality, the Assembly of the Serbian People was established. Now, to clear up the terminology, Assembly of the Serbian People is distinct from the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza which was created during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the eve of the war, I would say, the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. That's what I wanted to clarify. "Assembly of the Serbian People" does not mean that authorities have already been elected. If the Council of Serbian People had existed in Ilidza, do you think this assembly would have been formed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is my conviction that if you speak about the council of the people, it was one of the proposals to overcome the problems in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if the council of various peoples had been formed, I believe there would have been no creation of assemblies of the Serbian people anywhere in Bosnia, including Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This establishment of the assemblies, just the establishment of the Assembly of the Serbian People, not a Serbian municipality, was this disputed by the Muslims or was it accepted? Did it meet with their understanding? Sorry, before that: Was this done in secret or was it completely in the public domain and published in the media?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: As we can see from the newspaper, it was no secret, it was not clandestine activity. It was a very public act. And the next morning, I personally informed my colleagues in the Ilidza Administration, including my Muslim colleague Mr. Mahmutovic, that this had happened. I explained the context in which it had happened, and we both concluded that it would be necessary for this to be published. We agreed about that. We called the newspaper "Oslobodjenje," and that's how this was published, as one of preventive political steps that was to help find a solution for Ilidza municipality, and we were also hoping to set an example for other areas, other parts of Bosnia, to confront -- or, rather, prevent the things that happened later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have this document, P52534 [as interpreted], admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's already been admitted. I don't quite understand Dr. Karadzic's question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm looking for a new document, actually, P2534. It was a misinterpretation. We don't need this document anymore. It's been admitted. I just wanted Mr. Kezunovic to make a distinction between the Assembly of the Serbian People and the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza that was established only in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that correct? Do you agree with me, there is a distinction? The Serbian Assembly is something like a national council that is written into law nowadays, whereas the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza is something quite different; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already answered your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at this new document, and can we see page 4 in both versions. Let's first identify who the interlocutors are. On the 19th of February, 1992, I talked to my secretary in the Serbian Democratic Party, Mr. Grkovic. Can we look at page 4 in both Serbian and English versions. Okay: "Did he find Kezunovic?" We're looking at the lower portion of the text in both Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that I am trying to contact you, that I know your family name, but I don't know your first name, which also confirms that we had not had any private contacts before that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Everybody can see that. Can we go to the following page. Actually, 6 in Serbian, 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that Mr. Grkovic was aware of your moderate positions and views, and that somebody actually complained about you, and that I say that I don't believe that and that I say that you are always present and that you work well? Let me ask you, was it a generally-known fact that you were a very moderate person and that you were supported in your moderate views by the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I've never seen this transcript -- or, rather, I only saw it recently. I know Mr. Ljubo Grkovic, and from your conversation with him, I understand the context. And as for my activities in Ilidza, I did everything autonomously, as it were, and in that sense I did not have any objections coming from you, personally, or the Serbian Democratic Party. Nobody ever told me that what I was trying to do in Ilidza was wrong, that those activities were not in keeping with the policy of the SDS. At the end of the day, in that sense, I was not the only one. We can look at the example of Jovanovic and Maksim Stanisic, and some others as well. At that time, I was certain that I enjoyed the support of the party for all my activities. If that had not been the fact, I'm sure that the reactions would have been different. I was very active in the municipality, and I did not experience any objections coming from the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to ask you about the authorities of municipal bodies; primarily, the president of the municipality. You were close to him because you were the president of the municipal government. Can you give us an outline and tell us about the independence of the work of the president of the municipality, in terms of European charters as well as in terms of the tradition of our own self-governing socialism? And the document I would like to call up is 1D3498. And while we are waiting -- 1D3498. Is it true that our municipalities have always functioned in keeping with the European Charter on Local Self-Government, which was adopted in 1985, and that because of the previous self-governing socialism, our municipalities even enjoyed more independence than envisaged by the European Charter? It was adopted in 1985. You mentioned the charter earlier in your testimony, and that's why I'm referring to it now. It was adopted in 1985.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I described the authorities of the president of the Municipal Assembly, and those authorities stemmed from his election legitimacy. The president of the municipality was elected directly in municipal elections as the representative of the party that won the majority of votes in local elections. The president of the municipality was also the number-one man in the local community, and he was responsible for the overall activity in that municipality. There were also executive boards, as the executive bodies of government at the local level, which also had very clearly-defined authorities pursuant to the then Law on the State Administration that was in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The president of the municipality and all bodies of the local community had very well delineated and defined roles. And when we compare those today with the provisions of the European Charter on Local Self-Government, which was ratified twice in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the first time during the war and the second time after the war, I would say that they were a very close reflection of the provisions of the European Charter, which means they were adopted even at that time during the war. And I can describe that with only one word, the autonomy of local government, when it comes to making decisions on the issues of importance for that community.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go to the following page, and can we look at Article 4. Can you please throw a glance at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: One moment. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just a request for clarification, because hearing the witness, I understand him to be referring to municipality administrations pre-war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's what we need to determine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because if that's the case, I think this is completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The charter that was adopted in Europe in 1985, when the war started in Bosnia, was it the level of autonomy that our municipalities enjoyed? Please look at Article 4. Does this reflect the situation in our municipalities, irrespective of the fact when the charter was ratified? Do you agree that the former Yugoslavia ratified the charter even before Bosnia-Herzegovina became an independent state?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's a question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's probably true. But, in any event, I'm not sure this is going to help us very much, in terms of what we need to determine, Dr. Karadzic. I'd like to think about that over the break, which we're now going to take until 1.00. I just want to deal with one matter that arose earlier, when there was a discussion as to the admissibility or MFI'ing of D1251. And as a result of information I had, I thought it was consistent to admit it. I don't think that is accurate, and it was no fault of the advice which I received. But we shall MFI D1251, rather than admit it. 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you, Mr. Kezunovic: Did you have an opportunity to look at this additional information?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at the additional information, and it is correct. It reflects my words, it reflects what I said to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It will be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1252, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, the Defence has been given only three hours for the cross-examination. I requested 10 hours. I am hoping that the Trial Chamber will give me a bit more time, but we have to be efficient. Do you know that the SFRY had adopted the European Charter on the Local Self-Government?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, how is that relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If you can explain the relevance, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to confirm for us or deny and say what were the principles of the work of the municipalities and what was the relationship between the municipalities and the central government before the war and after the war started, until the moment when the witness was in power. This is a European document, and I would like the witness to say whether this document was ever adopted. The fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted it as an independent state is a different matter, but before that it was adopted by the former state of Yugoslavia, and I would like the witness to confirm that this was, indeed, the way municipalities functioned. And then we will see the link between central bodies of government and local bodies of government, and whether the local bodies of government were independent, and to what extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, the Judges will just confer on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The Bench will allow the question, but can we do it -- it can be done very expeditiously with "yes" or "no" answers, I suspect. I'm not putting that into the mouth of the witness. But if he can do it, one could see how it could very easily be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My next question: Do you know that Yugoslavia adopted and ratified this Charter on Local Self-Government before the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that ratification before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Ilidza municipality, were you familiar with this charter?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with it, and I can only speak on my behalf. I was familiar with these charters. And since I was the president of the Executive Board, somebody who worked at the level of local self-government on the eve of the war and after the war, when the European Charter was fully applied in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was in a position to compare the position of local self-government from before the war with what was happening after the war, when I was the mayor of East Sarajevo. And according to my assessment and evaluation, I thought that the position of local self-government in 1991 was fully compatible with the provisions of the European Charter on Local Self-Government. I'm not sure whether the charter was ever ratified in the pre-war Yugoslavia, but that doesn't change the fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be adopted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean, Dr. Karadzic. Do you mean adopt the European Charter on Self-Government?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Ilidza municipality and all the other municipalities function in compliance with that charter, I wanted it to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I see no alternative but to admit it in the circumstances, but for the limited purpose of confirming the question and answer that was given.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1253, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the witness tell us something about Article 4? Was that the basis for the functioning of the municipalities? Maybe we can narrow down the document. The document number or the exhibit number is 1D3498. Article 4 is on page 2. Please look at the first four articles, and can you tell us whether this was the basis for the functioning of our own local self-government? Did our local self-government function on these principles?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I -- can I just say, Your Honours, the witness has said time and again he can only refer to his own experience in Ilidza municipality, and he said it again with respect to this last question of Dr. Karadzic, yet Dr. Karadzic continues imposing broad-based questions here instead of listening to the witness and being responsive to his answer. I'd ask he rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, you have heard what the witness has said. He can only refer to his own position and his own locality, so we will assume the question is limited to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I try and answer the question, please? Your Honours, I would like to broaden my answer by adding to it one fact. My role was as the president of an association of cities and municipalities of the Republika Srpska. It is an association which expresses the interest of all local communes of Republika Srpska, and that was in 2005 and 2006. In that role, I was very close and very well informed about the application of the European Charter on Local Self-Government, in general, and especially in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that's why I'm in a position to be able to assess our own behaviour in 1991 with respect to the provisions that we applied in a later period. In my previous answer, I've already stated that even then in 1991, we applied the key provisions of the European Charter. I've already explained what those were. I've also explained our autonomy, and that was the standard adopted by the European Charter, which we adhered to in 1991. I had two different roles at that time, I still do, and I can say that we were autonomous, which is the main provision of the European Charter on Local Self-Government. In answering Mr. Karadzic's question, I would like to say that, yes, these are the provisions of the European Charter on Self-Government, and they reflect exactly what I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to put some yes/no questions to you. Do you agree that the authorities of a municipality and its bodies were stipulated by the Constitution of Yugoslavia and the Law on Local Self-Government; yes or no? My question was not recorded properly. Was it stipulated by the Constitution of the SFRY, Article 117, the Constitution of the SRBiH, the Statute on the Municipality and the Law on Local Self-Government? Are these the four documents that determine the position of the local self-government?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: These all seem to be things which can be matters of agreement, if they can be agreed. And, in any event, they also seem to me, at least, to be matters for expertise. I'm not sure how far this is going to get us, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't ask anybody who was not exercising the authority, but Mr. Kezunovic was a representative of the local government and knows the principle on which it operated. I just wanted this question to be answered: Was it regulated; whom did it report to; who could replace whom? And then we could move on after these questions are answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it may be simpler, simply, to ask the witness if he was behaving in a way which he considered to be in concert with the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, did your municipality function and did you personally operate in compliance with these documents, and do these documents regulate the conduct of local government?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: May I try to give an answer that is as brief as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, please try. Otherwise, I'm afraid we're going to stay here until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the local government was neglected as a local body of government in Bosnia and Herzegovina generally. "Local government" tried to become a constitutional category. The European Charter says local governments throughout Europe should be and must be constitutional categories, because this was not the case in the whole of Europe. And at the same time, I'm telling you that in pre-war Yugoslavia, the local government was a constitutional category at the level of the SFRY, at level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that sense, Yugoslavia was - how can I put it? - very contemporary in relation to the European Charter simultaneously. So in the role that I had, I was very familiar with those rules, and we were very pleased with the position of local government in relation to state governments, and this was something that was guaranteed under the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the president of the government was responsible to the mayor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that each elected organ was responsible to the body that elected it and not to some higher body? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the main SDS board, including the president, did not have any power in relation to municipal government, other than moral and political authority? I am speaking about your municipality now.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this option was not available to influence the government in any other manner, in view of the clear legal and constitutional position of self-government. So the influence could only be carried out by the elected representative government, including those at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You, as a representative of power, could receive any kind of directives or instructions from the SDS party as to how you would work and the manner in which you would operate?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, directly -- or, actually, I'm sure that, specifically, such instructions from you or from the organ called the SDS Main Board is something that I do not recall receiving; I, myself, personally. So I did not receive any such things directly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the translation, so that is why I am -- do you agree that all the other autonomous activities and powers, the local government was responsible for social self-protection and territorial defence, which was something under the jurisdiction of the mayor, ex officio? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the municipality had its own sources of finance, to a degree, and it also received funds from the republican budget in order to be able to finance its own activities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was also an element of the European Charter that was applied in the then Bosnia-Herzegovina, the financial aspect, one of the key aspects of the European Charter, the financial independence of local government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the control by the republican organs mainly came down to the legality and constitutionality of the work of the municipal organs; it did not affect any other aspects of government?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the republican organs were not able to replace or call to responsibility the president of the municipality or any others whom they did not actually elect?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the election and the end of the mandate of stripping of office of the mayor was regulated by the statute of each individual municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the election law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 21 of your consolidated statement, you speak about the manner in which the SDS functioned. Did you have in mind the period of 1991 and 1992, when you were actually performing these duties, just after the war broke out and the first month that you were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm speaking about the relevant period from the 1st of January, 1991, until the 15th of May, 1992. All that I have said refers to that period. Nothing I say includes the period before or after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've seen here, in the intercept between Jovo Jovanovic and Maksim Stanisic, that there was a recommendation for people not to go to work. Is it correct that you, during a mission in order to calm down the situation in Sokolovic Kolonija, were arrested by paramilitary or armed groups who were in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I cannot say that this was an arrest. I can say that it was a temporary capture that lasted for one night, let's say, from 10.00 in the evening to 2.00 a.m. And I think that is the first capture that occurred in our territory. So in that sense, I am the first prisoner in Sarajevo, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this was before the war broke out, and that armed groups of Muslims appeared in the municipality even before that and then, and that you, in spite of your immunity, were captured, taken prisoner, and that this happened before the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, much before that. I'm saying that this happened in the second half of February, so it was a month and a half before the war broke out. There were no combat actions or any other reason for such an action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, perhaps briefly, can you explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm actually, Your Honours, completely lost as to whether we're talking about the capture being in the month of February or the presence of armed groups being in the month of February. It's completely incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I thought it referred to both, but I may be mistaken. I thought -- Dr. Karadzic, can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to ask the witness. I'm going to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Muslims, armed groups, would appear in the municipal building, take it over or occupy it, and that you spoke with your Muslim counterparts and went to the settlements to calm down the situation, and that on one of such occasions you were captured? Can you please tell us whether this is correct, what groups were these, and in which period did this happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not talking about a lot of events. I'm talking about two individual events, one, when armed persons unknown to me waited for me in the municipal building when I came to work, and after my intervention they explained that this was their attempt to occupy the municipal building, but they left in the spirit of co-operation and talks which I had already had with the mentioned Mr. Mahmutovic. This is something that happened once, so we cannot talk about several attempts to occupy the building. It just happened once. The second attempt or the second incident is the capture which happened during one night in Sokolovic Kolonija, and this is one single incident, and it ended definitely with an agreement between myself and Mr. Mahmutovic, and that regardless of the unpleasant situation that I have found myself in, we found a way to overcome it and to try to wait for some kind of solution or some kind of better solution, not only for us, but for Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you had gone to Sokolovic Kolonija in agreement with Muslims -- with the Muslim president of the municipality and his chief of police. You went with the Serbian chief of police in order to calm down the situation, and this is where you were captured; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We -- this was our practice: We tried to preserve the territory of the Ilidza municipality and tried to prevent misunderstandings. Unfortunately, this incident that we're talking about now occurred in such a way that our successful practice until then was interrupted because it was an event of such a nature. Even though the act of my capture was unsuccessful, the result of our talks after that night was to attempt to postpone misunderstandings in Ilidza as much as this was possible and as much as it was up to people who were at the head of the municipal administration and to people who were at the head of the then police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did they treat you, those people who captured you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the details are really not that important, but it was something -- an event where I was mistreated, I was hit, something that happens throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina or anywhere else in a similar situation. It was a very unpleasant situation for me that night. However, I found strength to overcome it and, in a way, to forget about it, with the goal of trying to postpone any misunderstandings happening in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3494, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As opposed to the Assembly of the Serbian People, is it correct that in early May -- from April to early May, the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza and Serbian territory was delineated in the existing municipality of Ilidza; is that correct? Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the document. I was not present when the decision was adopted, because by that time already, in a manner of speaking, I was not carrying out my posts -- my duties anymore, not completely. But I am familiar with the document when the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza was practically defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that only Serbian settlements were part of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza in the then municipality of Ilidza, and we can see that those settlements are listed here?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, when we were looking at the map and when I was trying to describe to the Trial Chamber the territorial compactness and the ethnic compactness of the municipality of Ilidza, this is something that is reflected in this decision, the territorial space of the municipality of Ilidza that was territorially and ethnically compact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the date now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the accused please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where it is said "the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza," is it understood that the Muslims, wherever it was possible, would form their own municipalities, and the Croats at Stup would also form their own municipality, and that this was pursuant to some political agreements and accords?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "is this something that is implied," I think that I would hesitate to use that term, because what I tried and what I wanted to achieve at the time was the territorial reorganisation of the then municipality, as well as the town, and what that implied was reaching an agreement or a consensus at the level of the three key important political factors. No consensus was in existence at the time, and I assume that similar decisions were being adopted among the Bosniaks in Hrasnica and the Croats in Hrasnica [as interpreted]. However, there was no consensus or agreement among the parties about that, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that up until the 22nd of April, there was shooting and there were skirmishes, and that the first major attack on Ilidza occurred on the 22nd of April, 1992? I'm sorry, excuse me. I would like to tender this document. Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Very well, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Page 84, line 13, should state "Croats in Stup."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I repeat the question. Leave the skirmishes aside. Were there any skirmishes before the 22nd of April? Was there any shooting against Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that, unfortunately, problems in Ilidza started on the day -- on the holiday of Bajram. That was the 3rd or the 4th of April, and there were daily skirmishes until the 22nd, shooting from guns to scare neighbours. That went on until the 21st. And then on the morning of the 21st, the first major attack against Ilidza was organised from Hrasnica, from the side of the Institute for Rehabilitation, and the first casualties were 11 people, among whom my neighbours, friends and colleagues, four of them I know personally from the Janic family, Stanko Stanic, and I won't enumerate the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When we talked, you informed us that an hour or two before the attack, itself, you were in contact with the then president of the municipality, the Muslim official, Mahmutovic, and you had a feeling that something was afoot. You were trying to diffuse the situation. Is that correct? You had a proposal to make, to proclaim Ilidza an open city?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the same spirit that I mentioned before, when I talked about our talks and attempts to diffuse the situation in Ilidza, we had that last conversation with Mahmutovic around 4.00 a.m. on the 22nd of April, just an hour or two before the attack. And then, as a last-ditch attempt, I suggested that the two of us together proclaim the territory of Ilidza an open place to deter hostilities, to prevent them, and that was the last proposal I made in my role that I had then in the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then started the artillery cannonade by the Muslim forces, followed by an infantry attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said 11 people were killed then. Were most of them civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were also armed soldiers who were trying to defend Ilidza that morning, and they did repel the attack. But there were also civilians among the casualties. I can speak from memory because I knew some of these people. Half of them were soldiers, half civilians, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the purpose -- what was the purpose of that attack from the Muslim side of Ilidza against the Serbian side of Ilidza? Was there any need for the Muslims to capture the Serbian part of Ilidza, at the cost of human lives?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Calls for speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. That's an enormously wide question, Dr. Karadzic, and I think it's best to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the second major attack against Ilidza happened on the 14th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the second attack was more comprehensive. It was an attack also from Stup, from the side of Otes, from Butmir, and from Hrasnica, and at that time there were some eight new casualties in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that from all the Muslim neighbourhoods, in the Serbian part of Ilidza and in the Muslim part, like Hrasnica and Butmir, they attacked from all sides from which they could possibly attack on the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of that attack, in terms of destruction and casualties?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned that, too. I believe eight people were killed, and there was a lot of destruction; buildings, private houses, infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Pofalici was a Serbian neighbourhood that remained isolated, completely encircled by the Muslims in the centre, and it was attacked on the 16th of May and completely devastated?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I cannot speak at that time of the effects of the attack on Pofalici, but I know that refugees came from Pofalici to Ilidza via Zuc and Vogosca, and they shared very fresh impressions with all of us, including me, from those two days, the 15th and 16th of May, 1992, in the Sarajevo neighbourhood of Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kezunovic, in view of the large number of refugees from Croatia, did you already have at that time refugees in Ilidza who had come from Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure they were there at that time, but a bit later, yes, there was a whole enclave from -- of people from Zenica who had first moved to Otes and then after the war moved to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: By that time, the 14th, 15th and 16th, did refugees come from Sarajevo, itself; Pofalici, Dobrinja, Alipasino Polje, the adjacent neighbourhoods? Did refugees flow into Ilidza from the city of Sarajevo, itself?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, very briefly, these two attacks on Ilidza and the repercussions of the attack against Pofalici, how did that affect the population of Ilidza and the refugees who had already settled there? In other words, did you have problems with the people who, under the impression of all these attacks, were in communication with the authorities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I've already tried to explain. General panic prevailed in Ilidza. There seemed to be absolutely no prospects, and that made the situation unbearable for me. I felt I could not any longer continue to be responsible for the situation in Ilidza, and that's why, on the 15th of May, I wrote my letter of resignation to all my duties, because of the situation in Ilidza and the complete hopelessness of any efforts and all the ideas that I had until then believed in as the only possibility to avoid war in our region as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1086 is the next document I would like to call. It's an intercept of a conversation between Prstojevic and Milenko Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under those circumstances on the evening of the 15th, when you have new casualties among civilians, this conversation took place. Please look at it, and tell us, do you see the panic and the crisis you've just described reflected in the tone of this conversation? First of all, do you see where it says: "Good evening," in line 4? Is it a conversation that took place in the evening of the 14th of May, after this second attack?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see from the transcript that Mr. Prstojevic says in line 4: "Good evening."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in Serbian, and I believe it's also page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree there is reference to people in Kotorac, and Prstojevic asks if they had been arrested? Was Ilidza also attacked on that same day from the direction of Kotorac? Is Kotorac a small area just next-door to Butmir? Was it one of the points from which the Muslims attacked?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard or saw this intercept before. And as for what happened on the 14th of May, I already said that it was an all-out attack on Ilidza from all directions, and that means including Butmir and Donji Kotorac. So it was also aimed at this western side of Ilidza that is surrounded by Donji Kotorac, Butmir, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Read through to the end. Read, in fact, the whole intercept, and then I'll ask my question. Next page, please. Do you agree that in his rage, Prstojevic says, "We'll clear out Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica"? Did Serbs, in fact, attack Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica, or were these just words that never materialised?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is only one period about which I can testify. I've already said it was up to the 15th of May. And in that period, there were no such attacks against these places. It would be irrelevant to hear anything from me about the period later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know the other people in government in Ilidza. Did Prstojevic, or anyone else there, have the intention of expelling Muslims and Croats from Ilidza, and was any action ever taken for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's rank speculation you're asking the witness to engage in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm just wondering about that. Maybe that question wasn't exactly posed so artfully, but we've had many testimonies from UN personnel that they believe that shells were intended to terrorise the civilian population or what the intent was. And someone who was on the scene, who was a direct participant, knew the people involved, I think, could enlighten the Trial Chamber as to maybe not exactly directly what another person intended, but as to whether the expulsions were the result of somebody's -- that's what they regarded as a desirable outcome, or whether there were other reasons for it. So perhaps you could give Dr. Karadzic some latitude, because I think the witness is in a position to give you information on that issue that could be very helpful to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Robinson, it's one thing for a person to assess the effect of, for instance, direct fire by artillery, but it's another thing to ask him to go into the mind of another person. So if Dr. Karadzic can formulate the question in a way that doesn't require speculation, but simply is asking the witness for his impression of what happened as a result of a particular attack, then that could be relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Kezunovic, you know Mr. Prstojevic and you know other members of that government. Were you able to ever gain any knowledge -- did you ever hear of any intentions on their part to drive anyone out of Ilidza? Was there such a policy in existence in any quarters in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Right. I know Mr. Prstojevic, and I knew him very well; not only him, but all the people who held any posts of importance in Ilidza or had any influence. From what I know about the areas with a concentration of Serbs, and I can say the same about the areas populated by Muslims and Croats, the basic policy was to defend one's own families and territories where they were compact: Vojkovici, Krupac, Grlica, the centre of Ilidza, Blazuj, Serbian area; Hrasnica and Kolonija being the Muslim area; and Stup, the Croat area. I don't remember hearing, and if I had, I would have reacted as I did react in such situations. If I had ever heard of any conquering -- of any ambitions of conquest or expulsion, I would have reacted. But this was all about defence, self-defence from the other parties, and that also applies to the judgements and words of Prstojevic in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
