utterances.text: Can you say, briefly, yes or no, at the beginning of war, in this chaos, did Serbs and Muslims and Croats alike leave Ilidza of their own accord in certain numbers?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, panic reigned supreme. There was fear, there was hopelessness, and whoever had an opportunity to move their familiar out of Ilidza, they did that. And one of those who did that was me. I moved my family to our weekend house in Pale. I wanted to separate them from Ilidza, because I considered Ilidza a very difficult area, where future events were very unpredictable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that a considerable number of Muslims and Croats stayed in Ilidza and that a number of Croats moved into Ilidza from the areas in the direction of Kiseljak once the situation in Ilidza stabilised?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course people stayed in Ilidza, irrespective of their ethnic background. For example, my first-door neighbour, Husein Cehic, who stayed in Ilidza throughout the war, despite all the traumas that he experienced during the war, and then Katica, who was wounded in Ilidza and still remained living in Ilidza. There were a lot of examples like that. There were people who shared the destiny of Ilidza because they probably did not have an alternative. They couldn't do anything else, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up D1164 just briefly to see -- D1164. This is a UN document dated 15th September 1994. Page 4 -- let's first look at the title page. The document has been admitted. D1164, 15 September 1994. Can we go to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where it says: "The movement of people," here the United Nations inform that the ICRC witnessed when 100 Serbs were stopped on the road, and then the last sentence says: [In English] "The authorities may offer exchange for Muslim residents in Ilidza." [Interpretation] This means that the exit of the Serbs from Hrasnica is conditioned by the Muslim authorities by the release of Muslim detainees. Is this evidence that there was a considerable Muslim community living in Serbian Ilidza in 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot speak of any documents of the United Nations, but since I lived in Ilidza throughout the war and I personally knew people of different ethnic background, I've already mentioned two examples of my first-door neighbours who lived in Ilidza throughout the war, and at the same time I heard and I witnessed attempts of exchanges similar to the one mentioned in this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Milomir Soja, from Ilidza, who was a witness here, testified that he was a member of a delegation that went to Muslim families to pacify them, to encourage them to stay in Ilidza. While you were a member of the local government in Ilidza, did Muslims and Croats have an address that they could go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If Dr. Karadzic is going to refer to previous testimony, I'd like to have a page reference, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic, this is another example of what's happened on numerous occasions. Can you please provide a page reference when you're going to quote from a testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I would do that if I were given not ten, but at least six hours. I would be really precise. I'm trying to bridge the lack of time. But let's not talk about Mr. Soja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could Muslims or Croats talk to either you or to somebody else, and did they, indeed, talk to you in order to feel safe, given the chaos that prevailed and the large number of refugees that had arrived?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that during the time I was in Ilidza, I had daily conversations with people who resided at Ilidza at that time, and that included residents of different ethnic backgrounds. They would come to me, asking me to try and influence or find a solution for them to be cared for, or to organise their departure or transfer to a different territory, and so on and so forth. Unfortunately, my options towards the end of my activities were very limited at the time, unfortunately, and I could do very little to meet the requests of those people, who were afraid for their lives, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to briefly talk about the phenomenon of crisis staffs. Unfortunately, we don't have much time, so I would invite "yes" and "no" answers. Am I right in saying that the term "crisis staff" is something that was connected with any natural disaster, floods, fires, earthquakes, and that also includes wars; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Should we make a distinction between the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Democratic Party that was in a position to report on events from the Crisis Staff of the municipality as a government body?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about two different bodies. The first was a political body, and the second -- the latter was a government body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was membership in crisis staffs usually ex officio and stemmed from their positions in the government, and did these people represent the government in the crisis staffs to which they were appointed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it customary for a crisis staff to report to the regular bodies of authorities? Was it customary for the crisis staff to inform the bodies of government of their decisions when those bodies of government could be convened? For example, the municipality Crisis Staff or the War Presidency, when they took a decision at their session, were they duty-bound to report on that decision to the Municipal Assembly for such decision to be ratified by the latter body?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can only say that my answer would be, yes, in principle. However, during the period while I was in office and while I participated in the work of the Crisis Staff, there were examples when the work of the Crisis Staff was monitored and reported on by the Assembly of the Municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we say that the Crisis Staff of Ilidza was completely autonomous and independent in its work? Was it independent in its work? Could somebody dictate the Crisis Staff what decisions it would take?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff reported only to the Municipal Assembly. When it comes to Ilidza municipality and when it comes to the time when I participated in the work of that body, nobody could dictate the body what decisions to take, or at least I didn't know of any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we then say that a crisis staff is a form of concentrated municipal authorities, with a view to taking rapid decisions in situations when 15-day dead-lines could not be complied with? Is this just a form of concentrating the existing authorities because members of the Crisis Staff were all appointed ex officio and they were all members of the existing government? Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, the Crisis Staff was established in order to provide for efficient work, because the ordinary bodies of government would have been very slow and not very efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Crisis Staff in Ilidza was not a generator of ethnic cleansing, that it didn't take any decisions that would be in breach of any laws, at least during the period of time while you were in office? Especially, it didn't take any decision of that sort with regard to people of other ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: While I participated in the work of the Crisis Staff, I cannot talk about illegal decisions, especially not decisions that would have been taken against the population of other ethnic backgrounds. At the same time, there were some decisions that I either opposed or was -- or abstained in their passing because I believed that the Crisis Staff had to try not to compound the situation in Ilidza even further. I thought that the Crisis Staff had to try and relax the situation as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just for linguistic purposes, you say here that you cannot talk about illegal decisions. Does that mean that you don't know that any illegal decisions were ever taken? Is that what you meant when you said that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you know, the existence or the functioning of the Executive Board, was that part of a criminal intention, or a criminal organisation, or was it a way for the local self-government to organise itself? I said "Executive Board," but I meant the Crisis Staff. Was the Crisis Staff part of a criminal plan, a body that received its instructions from somebody else, or was it a way to deal with the problems that existed at the time on behalf of the government, as its concentrated form?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the first part of that multi-barrelled question about whether the Crisis Staff was part of a criminal plan isn't appropriate for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Not only that; the witness has already said, in very clear terms, what he thought the functioning and the necessity was for the Crisis Staff, so I think the whole question is, frankly, superfluous, Dr. Karadzic. Ms. Edgerton, while -- I'm looking at the clock. What's the -- what, if any, time would the OTP need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask for 10 minutes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The position is that Dr. Karadzic's three hours don't expire until 2.30, in any event. Dr. Karadzic, will you need to take the whole of that time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. I was hoping for more time, actually, but that would mean that we would have to keep Mr. Kezunovic until tomorrow, because I only touched upon a lot of the issues. And the gentleman who was the president of the Executive Board - that was the executive government at the time - could certainly tell us more. If we could extend today's work until quarter to 3.00, I am sure that both the Defence and the Prosecution could finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'll be advised if that is possible. That means the co-operation of all concerned. In the meantime, while that's being thought about, can you continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about your experience and about what you know about links and co-ordination between local self-government, more specifically your municipality, with republican bodies. Was there a link? Was there any co-ordination between the local level of self-government, and I'm talking specifically about Ilidza, and the central bodies of the Republika Srpska, at least during the period that you're familiar with, at the moment when the war broke out and for about a month and a half into that war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: The basic chains of communication from Ilidza and from all the other 10 urban municipalities were communication and co-ordination at the level of the city of Sarajevo. And in practical terms, all the administrative activities at the local level in Sarajevo boiled down to co-operation and co-ordination with the city. There were also co-ordination attempts with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina up to the spring of 1999. We, as local self-government, tried to deal with some large infrastructural problems that surpassed the abilities of both the municipality and the city. When it comes to the period leading up to the war, from the moment when the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, the municipal bodies, and I, as their leader, and, mind you, this was a newly-established administrative body, could not exist -- or, rather, no serious forms of co-operation could exist at the time, because very soon thereafter all the communication chains were severed. So in that sense, I can't talk about any type of subordination, co-ordination, or co-operation with the bodies that were established at the level of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your examination-in-chief, you mentioned a meeting which took place on the 17th of April. That was my only visit to Ilidza. Do you agree with me that the purpose of that meeting was to pass a decision on whether the central bodies of the Republika Srpska could be accommodated in Ilidza, and that the ensuing vote did not yield a decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, just to interrupt, but it's been confirmed that we can run until quarter to 3.00, but only until quarter to 3.00. So I would ask you, if you could, to finish your cross-examination by 2.35, and that gives 10 minutes for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I believe I can achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that voting took place and that the result of the vote was 4-4, which is why we did not take a decision at the end of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: The decision was not taken. The Serbian ministers in the government - there were eight of them present - could not agree, and that's why a decision was made by an inner circle, which included yourself. And we were informed at the meeting that you mentioned, that I attended in Ilidza, that there were no elementary security conditions in place for the bodies of the Serbian republic to continue working in Ilidza, which is why the bodies of government would move to Pale, and that was the result of that meeting which took place on the 18th of April, I believe, on the 18th of April, 1992, in Ilidza, the meeting that you and I both attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Three days thereafter, there was a big attack.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the meeting was not convened because of the citizens of other ethnic backgrounds? However, we did talk about them, and do you remember that I gave you some recommendations with this regard?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I can remember that meeting. For us in Ilidza, that meeting was very significant, and we in Ilidza had expected -- we wanted the bodies of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to continue working at Ilidza. When you took a different decision, we in Ilidza, including myself, were very disappointed. However, at the same time, I remember that meeting because of your words, because of what you said. You suggested -- you told us how we should behave in Ilidza, in view of the overall atmosphere. Your statement -- I cannot quote your words, but, in any case, you told us to organise ourselves so as to protect everybody, especially members of other ethnic groups. I believe that you spoke -- you uttered words to that effect, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry we don't have time to show that map. However, perhaps you can confirm for all of us that Ilidza was also completely surrounded by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In answering the Prosecution's questions, I described the atmosphere -- or, rather, what was happening throughout the war in Ilidza. I described the atmosphere in Ilidza as being very similar and riddled with the same problems as besieged Sarajevo. In that sense, Ilidza was doubly surrounded. On the one side, we had Sarajevo. On the other side, there was the area of Central Bosnia, leading towards Kiseljak. And in that sense, the territory of Ilidza was almost besieged in the same way as Sarajevo, and Sarajevo is the epitome of a surrounded city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Mount Mojmilo, towering above Ilidza, was the place from which they shelled Ilidza, Nedzarici, and other places in the depth of the territory? I could enumerate a number of localities, and the Trial Chamber now knows where they are. Can you tell me, just yes or no, did Muslims shell Ilidza from Mojmilo, and is Mojmilo the mountain towering above Ilidza; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know. But Igman was much more important, in that sense, as a place from which there is a better view of the entire territory of Ilidza. When we're talking about Mojmilo, yes, fire was opened from there, but not only on Ilidza, but also Vojkovici, Milici, Krupac, the so-called eastern part of the municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I started with Mojmilo. I would have arrived at Mount Igman. But could they shell you from Mojmilo, from Lanjaca [phoen], from Svabino Brdo, Sokoljevo, Igman? And I don't know whether they could shell you from Ormanj, but they could do it from Igman. Could they open fire at you from all the surrounding hills, and did they do it practically every day?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I would also include Ormanj, because in that part of Ilidza, in the western part of Ilidza, and I mean Zenik, Vela, and part of Rakovica towards Kiseljak, there was an area which was heavily shelled from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D3493.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the War Presidency of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza making a statement, a communique, dated 29 October 1992, at the time you were at the factory, not in government. Are you familiar with this incident of shelling of Ilidza, causing massive casualties among people standing at a bus stop, nine dead and thirty-five or thirty-three wounded?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's not nine; it's 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I did say 18.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I've already mentioned my neighbour, Katica, who was wounded, precisely in that incident, and of course I know about this horrible event that day at Ilidza, and I know four or five of them personally. Let me mention Lazar Sarenac, my friend, who was wounded seriously that day, my neighbour Katica. I'm very well informed of this horrific event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: At the factory Famos in Vojkovici, 29 October 1992. That's on the other -- the eastern side. On that day, I was not in this part of the centre where this happened at a bus stop, but it was very close to my apartment, and most of those people were known to me, my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember another major massacre when a wedding party was deliberately targeted near the church in Blazuj, causing, again, a number of deaths?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, not only near the church in Blazuj. I believe some 100 metres from the church, there was a hospital run by an enterprise called Put. It was targeted by shelling several times, and the patients were injured. Both the church and the hospital are in Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You, the municipal authorities, established that hospital when you were cut off from communicating between Kasindol and Ilidza. Was that a hospital that served both Muslims, Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The first part of that question is a statement, so maybe the witness could answer both of those, the statement and the actual question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The establishment of that hospital called "Zica" was necessitated by our inability to go to the hospital in Kasindol. Late Professor Miro Njego, we were looking for an adequate building, and we found one provisional building which we called "Zica," and we tried to find a few doctors. We found a group of doctors, headed by Dr. Pejic, to organise a field hospital, a make-shift hospital that would deal with the wounded. It was first on a hill near Blazuj that was later moved to the administrative building of that enterprise Put, and that hospital was shelled and attacked several times. So with regard to both make-shift hospitals on both locations, called "Zica," is something I negotiated with Dr. -- with Miroslav Njego.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that this hospital served Serbs, as well as Muslims and Croats, and even the injured of the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know. And I know personally the director of that hospital, Dr. Miroslav Pejic, and I talked to him frequently, trying to help the hospital, in my various roles, including the director of that factory. I got that information from him; namely, that his hospital in Blazuj served villages from Kiseljak, and Muslims and Croats from the surrounding area, and anyone who showed up at the door of the hospital and needed medical attention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that document is -- my objection, actually, is that that document is tu quoque and, therefore, irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hardly agree with this theme of Ms. Edgerton. This is not a tu quoque thing, it's not looking for a reason for Serbs to respond. Ilidza has an advantageous position. People were hit at a bus stop. It's not a justification for any action. There was no action. It says in the third paragraph that Serbs from Ilidza never reached out for somebody else's territory. This document just shows what the circumstances were and how much the Ilidza people suffered, and it has great relevance to the state of mind of the people and individuals in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it's relevant in this context: The relevance to the testimony of the witness. And in that respect and in that respect only, we are agreed that it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1255, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3490 is the next document I would like to ask for. 1D3490.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a document by Dr. Pejic, whom you mentioned, and it confirms he's asking the municipality to give more funding because of late -- pursuant to a decision of the civilian and military authorities, over the past five months they provided complete medical and surgical assistance to the population and troops of HVO Kiseljak. So they treated both the wounded and prisoners of war. Do you see in this document that the good doctor is asking the municipality to pay for that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak to this document because I am not familiar with it. But I've said in my previous answer, because I know Milan Pejic and talked to him frequently, and this document shows something that I was well aware of, and I and my colleagues, directors of various businesses in Ilidza, were trying to help the operation of that hospital and help the efforts of Dr. Pejic to do his work. In that period, I got information directly from him that the hospital catered both to the villagers and the civilian population, but even the military patients.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be received? And since I've exhausted all my minutes, I'm not going to continue, although there are many more topics and documents outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, as to admissibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, the witness said he couldn't speak to it, but then he offered an answer that assists Your Honours in interpreting the document. So no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you, Dr. Karadzic. That concludes your cross-examination. Now, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We just need an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit D1256.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, today in the transcript at pages 79 and 80, you engaged in an extended discussion with Dr. Karadzic - not from your statement, but from the transcript - about municipal government and political authority. And I'd actually like to take that discussion down from the rather abstract constitutional level it was at to the actual political and party structures that figure in your testimony. Your indulgence for a moment. I'd like to know, from your experience, from what you heard, from what you saw, did the SDS influence and even instruct its party members on the local level to act or vote in a particular manner?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question, but my answer would be that the SDS, as a political party, operated like any other political party. Through its membership, they tried to exert influence on various organs, executive boards, or local governments, or non-party figures like me, to realise their political intentions. I believe that is the case with all political parties in any system.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. One question relating to the note about the proofing session that was admitted here as D1252. That was the note that the Office of the Prosecutor prepared following your meeting with us yesterday. At page 83 of today's transcript, lines 18 to 22, Dr. Karadzic put to you that you went, with the Serb police chief of Ilidza, to Sokolovic Kolonija with your counterparts, Mr. Mahmutovic and Mr. Mlivic, and you actually agreed with him. Now, perhaps we could see that document, 1D252 [sic], because paragraph 14 of that document notes you as saying that the Serb police chief of Ilidza did not accompany you to Sokolovic Kolonija, and perhaps you could tell us which is, in fact, correct. Could we see quickly D1252, please, paragraph 14. If I can draw your attention to the fifth line of paragraph 14, it says: "The witness travelled to --"

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] But Kovac did not come.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you said to Dr. Karadzic, when you agreed with him that the Serb chief of Ilidza, went to Sokolovic Kolonija, that actually, you were mistaken; is that right? Mr. Kovac did not come?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly didn't say anything of the sort, that Kovac had come with me. It must be a mistake on the transcript. I couldn't have said that, because Mr. Kovac, although he was supposed to appear there, did not show up, although he had been properly informed. The fact is Mr. Kovac was not there, and if it says in the transcript that he was, it must be a typo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation came through "Chief Kovac." He was never chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kovac was never the chief. The chief was Mlivic -- Glivic, Glivic, Nedin Glivic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Finally, at pages 63 and 64 of the transcript today, you enumerated a list of the outlying neighbourhoods of Ilidza, describing their ethnicity, and you pointed out the population of the city centre was ethnically mixed. And then at page 84, Dr. Karadzic put a document to you from May 1992, D1254, saying that the Serb Municipality -- or dealing with the delineation of the Serb Municipality of Ilidza. Now, I note from this document that this central area, which you've described as being ethnically mixed, is actually included within the municipal boundary of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza, so I'd like to know what happened, then, to non-Serbs living and working in this central area.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The central part of Ilidza was ethnically mixed. It was even difficult to estimate the ethnic proportions of various groups. I suppose there was a slight majority of Serbs, slightly less Bosniaks, and a minority of Croats, but the central part of the municipality was ethnically very mixed. And in that whole situation, that was another factor that complicated it even further, and that fact also dictated and narrowed down the options for action in such an area. And there were incidents, like taking the flags down off the building of the municipalities, and other attempts -- we had to deal with any attempt to frighten members of different ethnic communities. And we always, in the government, tried to make sure the citizens knew that their ethnic group enjoyed equal protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How effective was that protection? What happened to the non-Serbs living and working in that central area?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: The war happened to them, and all the unfortunate circumstances war brings. And it brought them to Ilidza, like it brought them to the Serbs in encircled Sarajevo, especially in the initial -- the early days of the war, when there was no legal protection for anyone, before the police and then the army was established. But the early period, April/May 1992, was a period of complete chaos in Ilidza, where the situation was very hard for the non-Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think my time's up, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber would like to thank everybody involved in the extension of time, and in particular to you, Mr. Kezunovic. That's the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give it. You're now free to go, and have a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: 9.00 a.m. tomorrow morning. Thank you.
